interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @SpringBootApplication bundles @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan. Auto-configuration supplies beans conditionally, based on what is on the classpath and what you have already defined.
tips: The killer interview line: auto-configuration backs off when you define your own bean — @ConditionalOnMissingBean is the mechanism.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Spring Boot auto-configuration

commonMistakes: Putting business logic in controllers.
Returning 200 for everything, including errors.
Using GET with a body or POST for pure reads.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The DispatcherServlet is the front controller: it receives every request, consults handler mappings to find the matching @Controller method, resolves arguments (@PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody), and writes the response via message converters (JSON with Jackson by default). @RestController is @Controller + @ResponseBody — it returns data, not views. REST conventions: GET for reads (200), POST for creation (201 with a Location header), PUT for full replacement, PATCH for partial updates, DELETE for removal (204), and 404 for missing resources, 400 for invalid input, 401/403 for auth problems. Validate request bodies with Bean Validation (@Valid, @NotNull, @Size) and return field errors cleanly. Centralize error handling with @ControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler so controllers stay focused on happy paths. Keep controllers thin: they translate HTTP to service calls and back, and all business logic lives in services.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Spring MVC and REST in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: DispatcherServlet routes requests to @RestController methods. Use @GetMapping/@PostMapping with proper status codes, validate input, and handle errors centrally with @ControllerAdvice.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Spring MVC and REST

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Define an interface extending JpaRepository<Entity, Id> and Spring Data generates the implementation at runtime: save, findById, findAll, delete, plus derived queries parsed from method names (findByEmailAndActiveTrue). For anything the naming rules cannot express, write @Query with JPQL or a native query. Entities map tables with @Entity, @Id, @GeneratedValue, and relationships @OneToMany/@ManyToOne — fetch type matters: LAZY loads associations on access, EAGER loads them immediately, and lazy access outside a transaction throws LazyInitializationException. The N+1 problem (one query for parents, then one per child) is fixed with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection. Transactions belong on service methods with @Transactional (rollback by default only for unchecked exceptions), and read-only transactions (readOnly = true) are a cheap optimization for queries.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Spring Data JPA in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Spring Data JPA generates repository implementations from interfaces: derived query methods, @Query for custom JPQL, and @Transactional boundaries on services — with lazy loading and the N+1 problem as the classic traps.
tips: When asked about N+1, name the symptom (many small queries), the cause (lazy loading in a loop), and the fix (JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph) — all three in one breath.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Spring Data JPA in one minute

commonMistakes: Storing secrets or passwords in a JWT payload.
Accepting tokens without verifying signature or expiry.
Storing passwords in plain text or with a fast hash like MD5.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Authentication (who are you?) happens first, via login credentials, OAuth2, or a token; authorization (what may you do?) follows, via roles or authorities (ROLE_USER, ROLE_ADMIN). In Spring Security, a filter chain intercepts requests, an AuthenticationManager verifies credentials, and a SecurityContext holds the authenticated principal for the request. A JWT has three Base64URL parts: header (algorithm), payload (claims such as sub, roles, exp), and signature (HMAC or RSA over header + payload). The server verifies the signature with its secret or public key and rejects expired tokens — the payload is readable by anyone, so never put secrets in it. Access tokens are short-lived; refresh tokens (stored securely, ideally httpOnly) issue new ones. Stateless JWT auth scales because no server-side session is needed, but tokens cannot be revoked before expiry without a denylist — keep lifetimes short. Always serve auth over HTTPS, store passwords hashed with BCrypt (never plain or MD5), and protect against CSRF where cookies carry auth.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Security and JWT in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. JWT is a signed, stateless token: header.payload.signature — verify the signature and expiry, never trust the payload alone.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Security and JWT

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A microservice owns one bounded context and its own database — no shared tables across services, or you have a distributed monolith, not microservices. Services communicate synchronously (REST, gRPC) or asynchronously (events via Kafka/RabbitMQ); async messaging decouples services but introduces eventual consistency, so design for it (idempotent consumers, outbox pattern for reliable publishing). Cross-cutting concerns: an API gateway for routing and auth, service discovery for locating instances, centralized configuration, distributed tracing (trace IDs across calls), and resilience patterns — timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers. Spring Boot Actuator adds production endpoints: /actuator/health (liveness and readiness), /actuator/metrics (JVM, HTTP, custom counters via Micrometer), /actuator/info, and /actuator/env. Expose health publicly if needed, but restrict metrics and env behind authentication — they leak internals. Pair Actuator with Prometheus/Grafana for metrics and a log aggregator for logs.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Microservices and Actuator in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Microservices split a system into independently deployable services, each owning its data. Actuator exposes health, metrics, and info endpoints so you can observe them — but expose only what is safe.
tips: If asked 'monolith or microservices?', answer with trade-offs: microservices buy independent scaling and deployment but cost operational complexity — do not present them as always better.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Microservices and Actuator

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Records (Java 16) are concise immutable data carriers: record Point(int x, int y) {} generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString — use them for DTOs and value objects, not for mutable entities. Sealed classes (Java 17) restrict which classes may extend them (permits), making hierarchies exhaustive for switch expressions. Pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16) removes casts: if (obj instanceof String s) { use s directly }. Switch expressions (Java 14) return values and support arrow syntax, and pattern matching for switch (Java 21) matches on types and guards. Text blocks (Java 15) write multiline strings with """ without escaping every quote — ideal for SQL and JSON samples. var (Java 10) infers local variable types but is not dynamic typing and cannot be used for fields or method signatures. Virtual threads (Java 21) make blocking-style code scale to millions of threads, but do not fix shared-state bugs — synchronization rules still apply.
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Modern Java features in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Records for data carriers, sealed classes for closed hierarchies, pattern matching for instanceof and switch, text blocks for multiline strings, and var for local type inference.
tips: Name the Java version for each feature — interviewers use version numbers to check whether knowledge is current.
interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Modern Java features
Revision: SQL fundamentals
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: SQL fundamentals in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: SQL reads and changes data in relational tables: SELECT with WHERE filters rows, aggregates with GROUP BY and HAVING summarise them, and keys and constraints keep the data valid.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start from the shape of the data: a table has columns with data types, one primary key that uniquely identifies each row, and foreign keys that link rows in one table to rows in another. Constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT) are rules the database enforces so bad data cannot be saved. The everyday statements are SELECT (read), INSERT (add), UPDATE (change), and DELETE (remove), plus CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE for the structure itself. Filter rows with WHERE before they are grouped; use aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX with GROUP BY to summarise, and HAVING to filter the grouped results — WHERE cannot do that job because it runs before grouping. Order results with ORDER BY and limit them with LIMIT (or the equivalent in your database). For dates, know the basic date and time functions of the database you use, and remember that SQL is case-insensitive for keywords but the data itself may be case-sensitive depending on collation.
followUps: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
What does a primary key guarantee that a UNIQUE constraint does not?
When would you use DELETE versus TRUNCATE?
tips: Say the order of execution out loud: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT — it explains most SQL surprises.
commonMistakes: Filtering grouped results with WHERE instead of HAVING.
Forgetting that COUNT(*) counts rows while COUNT(column) skips NULLs.

interviewQuestions.title: Revision: SQL joins, subqueries, window functions and CTEs
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: SQL joins, subqueries, window functions and CTEs in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Joins combine rows across tables, subqueries nest one query inside another, window functions rank or total rows without collapsing them, and CTEs name a subquery so the main query stays readable.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Joins answer 'which rows go together?': INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows on both sides, LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills in NULLs where there is no match, and a SELF JOIN joins a table to itself (for example, an employee to their manager). UNION stacks result sets vertically and removes duplicates, while UNION ALL keeps them — the two queries must return the same number and compatible types of columns. A subquery is a query inside another query, in the SELECT list, the FROM clause, or a WHERE clause with IN or EXISTS; EXISTS is usually the better choice when you only need to know whether a match exists. Window functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) compute a value per row while keeping every row — unlike GROUP BY, they do not collapse rows, which is why they are the standard way to find the top N rows per group or a running total. A CASE expression adds if-then logic inside a query, and a CTE (WITH ... AS ...) gives a subquery a name so a long query reads top to bottom instead of inside out. When a query is slow, the first things to check are a missing join condition (which explodes into a cross product) and a missing index on the join or filter columns.
followUps: How would you find the second-highest salary in each department?
When would you use a subquery instead of a join?
What is the difference between ROW_NUMBER and RANK?
tips: For 'top N per group' questions, reach for ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY value) and filter on the row number — it is the answer interviewers expect.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the ON condition on a join and getting a cartesian product.
Using UNION when UNION ALL would do, paying for a sort and de-duplication nobody asked for.

interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Data types, variables and operators
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Data types, variables and operators in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Java has eight primitive types and reference types; variables hold values or references, operators compute with them, and casting converts between types — widening automatically, narrowing only with an explicit cast.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The eight primitives are byte, short, int, long, float, double, char and boolean; everything else is a reference type, including arrays and objects. Each primitive has a wrapper class (Integer, Double, Boolean and so on) used when an object is required, for example in collections, and autoboxing converts between the two automatically — but unboxing a null wrapper throws a NullPointerException, a classic interview trap. Local variables must be assigned before use, instance variables get default values (0, false, null), and final marks a variable that cannot be reassigned. Operators cover arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %), comparison, logical (&&, ||, !), and the ternary (condition ? a : b); remember that && and || short-circuit, so the right-hand side may never run. Type casting: widening (int to long, int to double) happens automatically and is safe, while narrowing (double to int, long to int) needs an explicit cast and can lose data — casting 9.9 to int gives 9, not 10. String concatenation with + converts operands to strings, so 1 + 2 + "3" is "33" while "1" + 2 + 3 is "123"; evaluation is left to right. Since Java 10, var lets the compiler infer a local variable's type, but the type is still fixed at compile time — it is not dynamic typing.
followUps: What happens when you unbox a null Integer?
Why does 1 + 2 + "3" give a different result from "1" + 2 + 3?
When is var allowed and when is it not?
tips: If asked about a tricky expression, evaluate it left to right and say each step out loud — that is how you avoid the string-concatenation trap.
commonMistakes: Unboxing a null wrapper and getting a NullPointerException.
Assuming a narrowing cast rounds instead of truncating.

interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Spring AOP
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Spring AOP in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: AOP moves cross-cutting concerns such as logging, transactions and security out of business code into aspects that Spring weaves around your methods.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Some behaviour cuts across many classes — logging, timing, security checks, transaction boundaries — and copying it into every method is noisy and error-prone. Aspect-Oriented Programming solves this by putting that behaviour in one place, an aspect, and letting Spring apply it where needed. The vocabulary: an aspect is the class holding the cross-cutting logic, a join point is a place it could apply (in Spring, a method execution), a pointcut is the expression selecting which methods (for example, all methods in a service package), advice is the code that runs (before, after, around, or when an exception is thrown), and the weaved result is a proxy around your bean. Spring AOP is proxy-based: it wraps your bean in a JDK dynamic proxy (when the bean implements an interface) or a CGLIB subclass proxy, and only public methods called from outside the bean go through the proxy — a method calling another method on the same object (this) bypasses the advice entirely, which is the most common AOP interview trap. @Around advice is the most powerful because it can run code before and after, change arguments, skip the call, or change the result; @Transactional itself is implemented as AOP advice. Keep aspects focused and pointcuts narrow: an over-broad pointcut advising everything is a performance and debugging headache.
followUps: Why does a method calling another method on the same bean bypass AOP advice?
What is the difference between JDK dynamic proxies and CGLIB proxies?
How is @Transactional related to AOP?
tips: The self-invocation trap is the AOP answer interviewers most want: advice only applies when a call goes through the proxy, never on this.method().
commonMistakes: Expecting advice to run on private methods or self-invocations.
Writing an over-broad pointcut that advises far more methods than intended.

interviewQuestions.title: Revision: Testing with JUnit, Mockito and MockMvc
interviewQuestions.question: Module 0 revision: Testing with JUnit, Mockito and MockMvc in one minute
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Unit tests check one class in isolation with JUnit assertions and Mockito stand-ins for its dependencies; MockMvc tests a controller's HTTP behaviour without starting a server.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A unit test checks one small piece of behaviour: arrange the inputs, act by calling the method, assert the outcome with JUnit 5 assertions such as assertEquals, assertThrows and assertTrue. Real dependencies make tests slow and flaky, so replace them with Mockito test doubles: @Mock creates a stand-in, @InjectMocks builds the class under test with those stand-ins injected, when(...).thenReturn(...) programs the stand-in's answer, and verify(...) checks a method was called with the expected arguments. Test the behaviour, not the implementation — a test that breaks every time you refactor the internals is a liability, not a safety net. For the web layer, MockMvc (with @WebMvcTest) sends fake HTTP requests to a controller and checks the status code, headers and JSON body without starting a server, while @SpringBootTest loads the whole application context and is reserved for integration tests that genuinely need it, ideally with Testcontainers for a real database. The test pyramid is the guiding shape: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few slow end-to-end tests. Name tests after the behaviour they check (for example, 'rejects an order with a negative quantity'), keep tests independent so they pass in any order, and never let a test depend on the current date, a random value, or an external service.
followUps: What is the difference between a mock and a stub?
When would you use @WebMvcTest instead of @SpringBootTest?
How do you test code that depends on the current time?
tips: If a test needs a real database or network, it is an integration test, not a unit test — say so, and name the right tool (Testcontainers, @DataJpaTest) for it.
commonMistakes: Mocking the class you are actually trying to test.
Writing tests that depend on execution order or on shared mutable state.

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: JDK is for development and includes the compiler and tools plus the JRE. JRE is for running Java and includes the JVM plus libraries. JVM is the engine that loads and executes bytecode, managing memory and garbage collection. Bytecode is platform-independent; the JVM is platform-specific, which is why the same bytecode runs on different operating systems with a JVM for each.
followUps: Is Java compiled or interpreted?
What does the bytecode verifier do?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: JDK is for developing (compiler + JRE), JRE is for running (JVM + libraries), and JVM is the engine that executes bytecode.
tips: Draw the nesting: JDK contains JRE, JRE contains JVM.
Mention bytecode portability explicitly.
interviewQuestions.title: JDK, JRE, JVM

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: String is immutable: operations like toUpperCase or concat return a new String instead of changing the original. This makes strings safe to share, safe as map keys (hashCode can be cached), and thread-safe. String literals are interned in the string pool, so two equal literals may share one object — but you should still compare contents with equals, not ==, which compares references.
followUps: When would you use StringBuilder instead?
Why is immutability important for HashMap keys?
interviewQuestions.question: Why is String immutable in Java?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: For security, thread safety, hashCode caching, and safe sharing — operations on a String return a new String instead of modifying it.
tips: Give a concrete example: a string used as a map key must not change after insertion.
interviewQuestions.title: String immutability

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A HashMap stores entries in buckets chosen by the key's hash. In Java 8+, a bucket starts as a linked list and converts to a balanced tree when collisions grow (8 entries with at least 64 buckets), keeping worst-case lookup from degrading linearly. Equal keys must have equal hash codes, and a key's hash code must not change while it is in the map — hence immutable keys are preferred. HashMap allows one null key; ConcurrentHashMap allows neither null keys nor null values.
followUps: What happens when two keys collide?
Why must equals and hashCode be consistent?
interviewQuestions.question: How does HashMap work internally?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Entries go into buckets by hash; buckets treeify under collision pressure in Java 8+, and keys must keep equals/hashCode consistent.
tips: Mention treeification threshold and the immutable-key rule — interviewers listen for both.
interviewQuestions.title: HashMap internals

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted, distinct) are lazy and return a new stream; they do nothing until a terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce, findFirst) runs. A stream is consumed by its terminal operation and cannot be reused — reusing it throws IllegalStateException. Short-circuiting terminals like findFirst or anyMatch can stop processing early.
followUps: When would you avoid parallel streams?
What is the difference between map and flatMap?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between intermediate and terminal stream operations?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Intermediate operations are lazy and return a stream; terminal operations trigger execution and consume the stream.
tips: Name one example of each, and mention that reuse throws IllegalStateException.
interviewQuestions.title: Stream operations

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Inversion of Control means the Spring container creates objects (beans) and supplies their dependencies, instead of each class creating its own with new. Dependency Injection is how it does that, preferably through constructors. Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, required, and final, and makes testing easy because you can pass a mock directly. Field injection hides dependencies and is discouraged in new code.
followUps: What is the difference between @Component and @Bean?
What happens when a prototype bean is injected into a singleton?
interviewQuestions.question: What is Inversion of Control, and why is constructor injection preferred?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: IoC means the container creates and wires beans; constructor injection is preferred because dependencies are explicit, required, final, and easy to test.
tips: Contrast with field injection explicitly — interviewers expect that comparison.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring IoC and DI

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Auto-configuration classes are guarded by conditions — for example @ConditionalOnClass (a class is on the classpath), @ConditionalOnMissingBean (no user bean of that type exists), and @ConditionalOnProperty. If you define your own bean of the same type, auto-configuration backs off for that bean. That is how Spring Boot provides sensible defaults that you can override. The --debug report shows which auto-configurations applied and why others did not.
followUps: What is a starter?
How do you debug a missing auto-configured bean?
interviewQuestions.question: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work, and how do you override it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Auto-configuration applies conditionally (classpath, missing bean, property); defining your own bean of the same type makes it back off.
tips: Mention @ConditionalOnMissingBean by name — it is the mechanism behind 'your bean wins'.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring Boot auto-configuration

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Loading N parent entities and then lazily loading a collection for each one produces 1 + N queries — the N+1 problem. Fix it with a fetch join (JOIN FETCH), an @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection that fetches exactly what is needed. Do not fix it by making everything EAGER, which loads data you may never use. Also, accessing a lazy collection after the transaction closes throws LazyInitializationException.
followUps: What is the difference between lazy and eager loading?
Why does @Transactional not work on a private method?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the N+1 problem in JPA, and how do you fix it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: 1 query for parents plus N queries for children; fix with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection — not blanket EAGER.
tips: Name the fix and the anti-pattern (blanket EAGER) in the same answer.
interviewQuestions.title: JPA N+1 problem

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: synchronized provides mutual exclusion and visibility: only one thread holds a given monitor at a time, and writes before releasing the lock are visible to the next thread acquiring it. volatile provides visibility only: writes are visible to other threads, but compound actions like count++ (read-modify-write) are still not atomic. For atomic single-variable updates, use AtomicInteger and friends, or a lock.
followUps: Why is a plain counter unsafe across threads?
What is a happens-before relationship?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between synchronized and volatile?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: synchronized gives exclusion plus visibility; volatile gives visibility only, not atomicity for compound actions.
tips: Use count++ as the concrete counterexample for volatile.
interviewQuestions.title: synchronized vs volatile

commonMistakes: Reaching for StringBuilder.reverse() when the question forbids built-in helpers.
Forgetting that strings are immutable, so you must build a new string rather than editing in place.
Off-by-one errors: using right = chars.length instead of chars.length - 1.
followUps: How would you reverse only the words in a sentence, keeping the word order?
What changes if the string can contain characters outside the basic multilingual plane, like emoji?
interviewQuestions.question: Write a Java method that reverses a string without using any built-in reverse helper.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Turn the string into a char array, swap characters from both ends towards the middle with two pointers, then build a new String from the array.
tips: Say the time and space cost out loud: O(n) time, O(n) space for the array.
Name the real-world shortcut (StringBuilder.reverse) even though the question forbids it — it shows you know both.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: reverse a string

commonMistakes: Counting 'Java' and 'java' as different words because the case was not normalised.
Using containsKey plus get in two lookups instead of getOrDefault or merge.
Forgetting that splitting an empty string returns an array with one empty string.
followUps: How would you find the most frequent word from the map?
How would you do the same counting with a stream and Collectors.groupingBy?
interviewQuestions.question: Write a Java method that counts how many times each word appears in a sentence, using a HashMap.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Split the sentence into words and count each one in a HashMap with getOrDefault(word, 0) + 1.
tips: Mention the O(n) time cost and why a map is the right structure: one pass, constant-time lookups.
Volunteer the LinkedHashMap variant if the interviewer asks about keeping word order.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: count words with a HashMap

commonMistakes: Comparing with == on strings instead of comparing characters.
Reversing the whole string first and then comparing — it works, but it uses extra memory for no reason.
Forgetting case: 'Madam' fails a plain comparison unless you normalise case first.
followUps: How would you check a sentence palindrome that ignores spaces and punctuation, like 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'?
How would you test a number for being a palindrome without converting it to a string?
interviewQuestions.question: Write a Java method that checks whether a string is a palindrome.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Compare characters from both ends towards the middle; the first mismatch means it is not a palindrome.
tips: State the complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space — better than reversing and comparing.
Mention the case-insensitive variant before the interviewer asks.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: palindrome check

commonMistakes: Sorting the array first: correct, but O(n log n) when one pass is enough.
Treating the second element of a sorted array as the answer, which fails when the largest value appears twice.
Using Integer.MIN_VALUE as a sentinel for 'not found yet' — it breaks if the array genuinely contains that value.
followUps: How would you find the third-highest distinct number?
How would you solve it with a stream, and what does that cost compared with the single pass?
interviewQuestions.question: Write a Java method that finds the second-highest distinct number in an array, in a single pass.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: One pass tracking the largest and second-largest distinct values; duplicates of the largest are ignored, and fewer than two distinct values is an error.
tips: Walk through [9, 9, 7] by hand — it proves you handled the duplicate-largest trap.
Say why you did not sort: O(n) beats O(n log n) here.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: second-highest number

commonMistakes: Writing a manual loop with a map and if-else when groupingBy does the same thing in one line.
Forgetting that groupingBy returns a Map, so you cannot call stream operations on the result directly.
Using groupingBy without a downstream collector when you only need counts — groupingBy(key, counting()) is the idiomatic form.
followUps: How would you find the department with the most employees from the grouped map?
What is the difference between groupingBy and partitioningBy?
interviewQuestions.question: How does Collectors.groupingBy work, and how would you use it to count items per group?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: groupingBy buckets stream elements into a Map by a key function; a downstream collector like counting() summarises each bucket instead of keeping a list.
tips: Give two examples: grouping into lists and grouping with counting() — interviewers often ask for the second.
Mention that the result map is a HashMap by default, so group order is not guaranteed.
interviewQuestions.title: Streams: groupingBy

commonMistakes: Using map on a list of lists and ending up with Stream<List<String>> instead of Stream<String>.
Forgetting that flatMap needs a function returning a stream — List::stream is the usual one.
Calling flatMap on a stream of arrays without Arrays.stream.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
map transforms each element one-to-one, so mapping a list of lists gives you a stream of lists. flatMap transforms each element into a stream and then flattens all those streams into one, which is what you want when each element itself holds several items.

```java
List<List<String>> nested = List.of(
    List.of("a", "b"), List.of("b", "c"), List.of("d"));

List<String> flat = nested.stream()
    .flatMap(List::stream)
    .distinct()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// [a, b, c, d]
```

The same pattern flattens other nested shapes: Optional::stream flattens a stream of Optionals, dropping empty ones, and Arrays::stream flattens a stream of arrays. A useful way to remember it: use map when one input gives one output, and flatMap when one input gives zero or more outputs.
followUps: How would you flatten a stream of Optionals and drop the empty ones?
What is the difference between flatMap and map followed by reduce?
interviewQuestions.question: What is flatMap, and how would you use it to flatten a list of lists into a single list?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: flatMap turns each element into a stream and flattens them into one stream — use List::stream to flatten a list of lists, unlike map, which would give a stream of lists.
tips: Use the 'one input, many outputs' rule of thumb — it answers most flatMap follow-ups.
Show distinct() in the example: it proves the flattened result is a plain list you can keep processing.
interviewQuestions.title: Streams: flatMap

commonMistakes: Using == to compare string contents — it sometimes appears to work because of the string pool, then fails on strings built at runtime.
Overriding equals without overriding hashCode, which breaks HashMap and HashSet behaviour.
Comparing objects with equals without a null check, risking a NullPointerException — use Objects.equals instead.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
== compares references: are these two variables pointing at the same object? equals compares contents: do these two objects hold the same value? For strings, "java" == "java" can be true because both literals share one pooled object, but new String("java") == "java" is false even though equals returns true — which is why you should always use equals for content.

The two are linked by a contract: if two objects are equal by equals, they must return the same hashCode. That is why you override both together. If you override equals but not hashCode, two equal objects can land in different HashMap buckets and a lookup will miss. For null safety, Objects.equals(a, b) handles nulls on either side. For primitives there is no equals, so == is correct — the confusion only applies to objects.
followUps: Why must equals and hashCode be consistent?
What does the string pool have to do with == sometimes working on strings?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between == and equals() in Java?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: == compares object references (identity); equals() compares contents (value). For objects, use equals() — and keep it consistent with hashCode().
tips: Give the string-pool trap as your example: literal == literal can be true, but new String == literal is false.
Mention Objects.equals for null safety — it is a small detail interviewers like.
interviewQuestions.title: == vs equals()

commonMistakes: Using StringBuffer everywhere 'to be safe' — the synchronisation costs speed and is pointless in single-threaded code.
Concatenating strings in a loop with +, which builds a throwaway String on every iteration.
Sharing one StringBuilder across threads without synchronisation.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
String is immutable: every 'change' creates a new object. StringBuilder and StringBuffer are both mutable alternatives for building strings piece by piece, and they differ in exactly one way: StringBuffer synchronises every method, so it is thread-safe but slower; StringBuilder has no synchronisation, so it is faster but not safe to share across threads.

In practice, use StringBuilder — almost all string building happens inside one method on one thread, where thread safety buys nothing. Use StringBuffer only when several threads genuinely append to the same buffer, which is rare. And never build a string in a loop with + : each + creates a new intermediate String, turning an O(n) job into O(n^2) copying, while a single StringBuilder appends in place.
followUps: Why is String immutable in the first place?
What happens if two threads append to the same StringBuilder?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between StringBuilder and StringBuffer, and when should you use each?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Both are mutable string builders; StringBuffer is synchronised (thread-safe, slower) and StringBuilder is not (faster). Use StringBuilder unless threads truly share the buffer.
tips: Lead with the one real difference — synchronisation — then the rule of thumb.
Mention the loop-concatenation trap: + in a loop is the classic reason this question comes up.
interviewQuestions.title: StringBuilder vs StringBuffer

commonMistakes: Saying final means 'constant' — it means the reference or value cannot be reassigned, but the object it points to can still change.
Thinking a final method can be overridden, or a final class extended.
Declaring every field final without thinking — final fields must be assigned exactly once, in the constructor or at declaration.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
final means 'cannot be reassigned or changed further', and what that blocks depends on where it sits. A final variable cannot be assigned a second time. A final method cannot be overridden in a subclass. A final class cannot be extended at all — String is final for exactly this reason, so nobody can subclass it and break its guarantees.

Two subtleties matter. First, final on a reference only freezes the reference: a final List can still have elements added to it, because the list object itself is mutable. True immutability needs a final class, final fields, and no methods that leak mutable state. Second, a final field must be assigned exactly once — at declaration or in every constructor — and a local variable used inside a lambda must be final or effectively final (never reassigned after it is set).
followUps: What is the difference between final, finally, and finalize()?
How do you make a class truly immutable?
interviewQuestions.question: What does the final keyword do in Java, for variables, methods, and classes?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: final blocks reassignment (variables), overriding (methods), and subclassing (classes). It freezes the reference, not the object it points to.
tips: Use the final List example — it shows you understand the reference-vs-object distinction.
Volunteer the effectively-final rule for lambdas; it connects final to modern Java.
interviewQuestions.title: The final keyword

commonMistakes: Saying interfaces are 'just abstract classes with no code' — since Java 8 they can carry default and static methods.
Using an abstract class when the goal is a capability shared across unrelated classes — that is what interfaces are for.
Forgetting that a class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Both define a contract that other classes fulfil, but they differ in what they can carry and how they combine. An abstract class can hold state (fields), constructors, and concrete methods, and a class can extend only one of them. An interface historically held only method signatures and constants; since Java 8 it can also hold default and static methods, and since Java 9 private methods — but still no instance fields or constructors — and a class can implement as many interfaces as it likes.

Choose an abstract class when the types share code and state and form one family — for example, an abstract PaymentProcessor with shared logging and a template method. Choose an interface when you are describing a capability that unrelated classes can share — for example, Payable implemented by an Invoice, a Subscription, and a Refund. When in doubt at 0–3 years, prefer the interface: it keeps your options open, and you can always add a default method later.
followUps: When would you use a default method in an interface?
Can an interface extend another interface, and can it have fields?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface, and when would you use each?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: An abstract class can hold state, constructors, and shared code but allows single inheritance; an interface defines a capability, allows multiple implementation, and since Java 8 can carry default methods.
tips: Give one concrete pair of examples (a family vs a capability) — it beats a list of differences.
Mention default methods explicitly so the answer does not sound pre-Java-8.
interviewQuestions.title: Abstract class vs interface

commonMistakes: Saying overriding is decided at compile time — it is decided at runtime from the actual object type.
Changing the parameter list in an override and accidentally overloading instead.
Narrowing the return type to an unrelated type, or making the overriding method more restrictive in visibility.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Overloading is several methods with the same name but different parameter lists in one class. Which one runs is decided by the compiler from the argument types — it is compile-time polymorphism. Overriding is a subclass replacing a parent method with the same name and the same parameters. Which version runs is decided at runtime from the actual object type — it is runtime polymorphism.

The rules differ too. An overload can change the return type and visibility freely, as long as the parameters differ; changing only the return type is not an overload and does not compile. An override must keep the same signature, may return a subtype (covariant return), cannot reduce visibility, and cannot throw new checked exceptions. Always write @Override on an overriding method: if you mistype the name or parameters, the compiler tells you instead of silently creating an overload.
followUps: Can you overload a method by changing only its return type?
Can a static method be overridden?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Overloading is same name, different parameters, resolved at compile time; overriding is a subclass replacing a parent method with the same signature, resolved at runtime.
tips: Say 'compile time vs runtime' first — that is the one line interviewers remember.
Mention @Override as a safety net against accidental overloading.
interviewQuestions.title: Method overloading vs overriding

commonMistakes: Assuming every bean is a singleton by design — singleton is just the default scope, not a guarantee of thread safety.
Expecting a prototype bean injected into a singleton to be fresh on every call — it is created once, at injection time.
Using request or session scope in a non-web application, where no request exists.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Scope controls how many instances of a bean the container creates and how long each lives. Singleton (the default) means one shared instance per container — the right choice for stateless services. Prototype means a new instance every time the bean is requested — the right choice for stateful, short-lived objects. In web applications there are also request (one per HTTP request), session (one per user session), and application scopes.

Two points catch people out. First, singleton beans must be thread-safe, because every request shares the one instance — keep them stateless or synchronise the mutable parts. Second, injecting a prototype bean into a singleton does not give you a fresh prototype per call: the container creates the prototype once, when it wires the singleton. To get a new one per use, inject an ObjectProvider or a Provider and call get() each time.
followUps: How do you get a fresh prototype bean inside a singleton?
Are singleton beans thread-safe?
interviewQuestions.question: What bean scopes does Spring provide, and which one is the default?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Singleton is the default (one shared instance); prototype gives a new instance per request, and web apps add request, session, and application scopes. Singletons must be thread-safe.
tips: Name the prototype-in-singleton trap — it is the most common follow-up to this question.
State the default first, then the others; interviewers check you know singleton is a default, not a law.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring bean scopes

commonMistakes: Saying BeanFactory and ApplicationContext are interchangeable — for most apps you want the ApplicationContext.
Manually creating a BeanFactory in application code instead of letting Spring Boot build an ApplicationContext.
Expecting lazy loading from an ApplicationContext, which eagerly creates singleton beans by default.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Both are IoC containers, but BeanFactory is the basic one and ApplicationContext builds on top of it. BeanFactory creates beans lazily — only when first requested — and offers just the core wiring. ApplicationContext eagerly creates singleton beans at startup, and adds the features real applications need: event publishing, internationalisation, resource loading, and integration with AOP and the web layer.

In practice, always use an ApplicationContext (Spring Boot creates an AnnotationConfigApplicationContext for you). Eager startup is a feature, not a cost: a misconfigured bean fails fast at startup instead of failing on the first user request. Reach for a plain BeanFactory only in a constrained environment, such as a tiny embedded tool where startup time and memory matter more than the extra features.
followUps: Which container does Spring Boot use?
Why is eager bean creation at startup a good thing?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between BeanFactory and ApplicationContext in Spring?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: BeanFactory is the basic, lazy container; ApplicationContext extends it with eager singleton creation plus events, messages, resource loading, and AOP/web integration. Use ApplicationContext.
tips: Frame eager startup as fail-fast — it turns a drawback into a design reason.
Name the concrete Boot container type if you can: AnnotationConfigApplicationContext.
interviewQuestions.title: BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext

commonMistakes: Treating @SpringBootApplication as magic — it is three annotations combined, and you should know which three.
Putting the main class in the wrong package so component scan misses your controllers.
Adding @ComponentScan with a broad base package that picks up beans from another module by accident.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
@SpringBootApplication is a convenience annotation that combines three others. @Configuration marks the class as a source of bean definitions. @EnableAutoConfiguration tells Spring Boot to configure beans automatically based on what is on the classpath. @ComponentScan tells Spring to find @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller classes in the current package and below.

The scan base matters: by default it is the package of the class carrying the annotation, so put your main class in the root package of your project (for example com.example.shop) so that com.example.shop.web and com.example.shop.service are all scanned. If a bean is not found at startup, a misplaced main class is the first thing to check. You can narrow or widen the scan with the scanBasePackages attribute, but the usual fix is to move the main class, not to add scanning config.
followUps: How does @EnableAutoConfiguration decide which beans to create?
What happens if two scanned classes define beans with the same name?
interviewQuestions.question: What does the @SpringBootApplication annotation do internally?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: It combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan — so the class defines beans, triggers auto-configuration, and scans its own package downwards for components.
tips: List the three annotations by name, then explain the package-placement consequence.
Mention the misplaced-main-class debugging tip — it shows real experience.
interviewQuestions.title: @SpringBootApplication internals

commonMistakes: Adding individual library versions by hand instead of letting the starter and its parent manage versions.
Including two starters that pull in conflicting versions of the same library without checking the dependency tree.
Treating a starter as a framework feature rather than a bundle of dependencies — it adds jars, not code.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
A starter is a pre-packaged bundle of dependencies for one job, with versions chosen to work together. spring-boot-starter-web brings Spring MVC, Jackson, validation, and an embedded Tomcat; spring-boot-starter-data-jpa brings Hibernate and Spring Data JPA; spring-boot-starter-test brings JUnit, Mockito, and AssertJ. You add one dependency instead of hunting down five compatible ones.

Versions come from the spring-boot-starter-parent (or the BOM): you declare the starter without a version and Boot supplies a tested one. That is why a starter keeps your build consistent — every starter in the same Boot release is tested against the same library versions. If you do hit a conflict, mvn dependency:tree shows which starter pulled in the unwanted version, and you override it with a property such as <jackson.version> or an exclusion.
followUps: What is the difference between spring-boot-starter-parent and spring-boot-dependencies?
How do you find which starter is pulling in a conflicting library version?
interviewQuestions.question: What are Spring Boot starters, and how do they simplify dependency management?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Starters are tested bundles of dependencies for one job (web, JPA, test); the starter parent supplies compatible versions, so you declare one dependency instead of many.
tips: Name three starters and what each pulls in — concrete examples beat a definition.
Mention mvn dependency:tree as the conflict-finding tool.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring Boot starters

commonMistakes: Enabling every actuator endpoint in production, including env and heapdump, without security.
Assuming Actuator is on by default — only health and info are exposed over HTTP out of the box.
Checking only that the app starts, instead of checking /actuator/health in a deployment probe.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Actuator adds production-ready endpoints to your app for health, metrics, and inspection. The most used are /actuator/health (is the app and its database up?), /actuator/info (build and version details), /actuator/metrics (JVM, HTTP, and custom counters), and /actuator/env and /actuator/beans for debugging. Add spring-boot-starter-actuator, and in recent Boot versions health and info are the only endpoints exposed over HTTP by default — the rest need management.endpoints.web.exposure.include to be switched on.

Two habits matter. First, wire /actuator/health into your deployment: a load balancer or Kubernetes liveness probe should call it rather than just checking the port is open. Second, treat the detailed endpoints as sensitive: env can leak secrets and heapdump can leak memory contents, so expose them only on an internal port or behind authentication, never on the public internet.
followUps: How do you add a custom health indicator?
How would you secure actuator endpoints in production?
interviewQuestions.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator, and which endpoints would you use in production?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Actuator exposes health, info, metrics, and inspection endpoints; use /actuator/health in deployment probes, and keep detailed endpoints like env behind authentication.
tips: Name the exact endpoints and the default-exposure rule (only health and info).
Mention the security warning — interviewers ask about it for actuator specifically.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring Boot Actuator

commonMistakes: Calling DispatcherServlet 'the controller' — it is the front controller that routes to your controllers.
Forgetting that @RestController methods skip view resolution and write straight to the response body.
Describing the flow without naming HandlerMapping or ViewResolver — interviewers listen for both.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
DispatcherServlet is the front controller: every HTTP request enters through it, and it coordinates the rest. First it asks a HandlerMapping which controller method handles this URL. Then it calls that method (through a HandlerAdapter), passing in request data bound to method arguments. The controller returns either a view name plus a model, or — for a @RestController — a body object. In the view case, a ViewResolver turns the name into a template (such as a Thymeleaf page) and renders it with the model; in the REST case, a message converter serialises the object to JSON and writes it to the response.

So the short version is: DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → controller → (ViewResolver → view, or message converter → JSON). Exceptions anywhere in that chain can be handled centrally with @ControllerAdvice. If a request returns 404, the usual suspects are a wrong mapping, a controller outside the component-scan package, or a missing annotation — all of which sit on this path.
followUps: What is the difference between a filter and an interceptor in this flow?
Where does @ControllerAdvice fit into the request lifecycle?
interviewQuestions.question: Describe the lifecycle of a request in Spring MVC, starting at the DispatcherServlet.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: DispatcherServlet receives every request, HandlerMapping picks the controller method, the controller returns a view name or a body object, and a ViewResolver or a JSON message converter produces the response.
tips: Recite the chain as an arrow sequence — it is easy to follow and hard to get wrong.
Mention the 404 debugging angle: wrong mapping or a controller outside component scan.
interviewQuestions.title: DispatcherServlet request flow

commonMistakes: Returning a plain string from a @Controller method and expecting JSON — it is treated as a view name.
Putting @ResponseBody on every method instead of using @RestController on the class.
Using @Controller for a REST API and wondering why the response is a 404 for a 'view' that does not exist.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
@Controller marks a class as a web controller whose methods usually return view names: return "home" and Spring resolves a template called home. @RestController is @Controller plus @ResponseBody on every method, so return values are serialised (usually to JSON by Jackson) and written straight to the response body instead of being treated as view names.

Use @Controller for server-rendered pages (Thymeleaf, JSP) and @RestController for REST APIs. The two are easy to confuse because they look identical — the difference is entirely in what happens to the return value. A common interview trap is a @Controller method returning a string like "success": Spring looks for a view named success and returns a 404 or an error page, while the same method in a @RestController would return the text success as the response body.
followUps: How do you return a specific HTTP status code from a @RestController method?
When would you use ResponseEntity instead of returning an object directly?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between @Controller and @RestController?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @Controller methods return view names to be rendered; @RestController adds @ResponseBody to every method, so return values are serialised to JSON and written to the response body.
tips: Use the 'return "success"' trap as your example — it makes the difference concrete.
Say which one you use for APIs and which for pages; interviewers want the rule, not just the definition.
interviewQuestions.title: @Controller vs @RestController

commonMistakes: Extending JpaRepository when you only need basic CRUD — CrudRepository is the simpler, sufficient choice.
Calling save() in a loop for thousands of rows instead of saveAll with batching.
Expecting findById to throw when nothing is found — it returns an empty Optional.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
CrudRepository is the base repository interface with the basic operations: save, findById, findAll, deleteById, existsById, and count. JpaRepository extends PagingAndSortingRepository, which extends CrudRepository, so it has everything CrudRepository has plus JPA-specific operations: flush, saveAndFlush, deleteAllInBatch, deleteInBatch, and getReferenceById, plus paging and sorting through Pageable and Sort.

For a 0–3 year interview, the rule is simple: reach for JpaRepository when you need paging, sorting, or batch deletes; CrudRepository is enough for plain CRUD. Both give you derived query methods for free — findByEmail(String email) becomes a query from the method name alone — and both let you add @Query methods for anything the naming rules cannot express. One habit to build early: findById returns Optional, so handle the empty case with orElseThrow instead of calling get() blindly.
followUps: How do you write a custom query with @Query?
What is the difference between deleteAll and deleteAllInBatch?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between CrudRepository and JpaRepository?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: JpaRepository extends CrudRepository (via PagingAndSortingRepository) and adds paging, sorting, flush, and batch-delete operations; use it when you need those, CrudRepository for plain CRUD.
tips: Draw the hierarchy: CrudRepository → PagingAndSortingRepository → JpaRepository.
Mention the Optional return of findById — it is the detail that shows you have used it.
interviewQuestions.title: CrudRepository vs JpaRepository

commonMistakes: Putting @Transactional on a private method or calling it from within the same class — Spring's proxy never sees the call, so no transaction starts.
Expecting a rollback for a checked exception — by default Spring rolls back only on unchecked exceptions.
Making every method @Transactional 'just in case', which hides real transaction boundaries and hurts performance.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
@Transactional marks a method (usually on a service) as one database transaction: either all of its writes commit together, or none of them do. If the method throws an unchecked exception (a RuntimeException), Spring rolls the transaction back; if it returns normally, Spring commits. That is the behaviour you want for a transfer that debits one account and credits another — a failure halfway must not leave the money debited but not credited.

Three rules decide whether it works. First, it only applies when the call goes through Spring's proxy, so annotate public service methods and call them from another bean — a private method, or a self-call inside the same class, runs with no transaction at all. Second, checked exceptions do not trigger rollback unless you set rollbackFor. Third, keep the transaction short and at the service layer, not the repository layer: a long transaction holds database locks and connections while your code does unrelated work.
followUps: Why does @Transactional not work on a private method?
How do you make a transaction roll back for a checked exception?
interviewQuestions.question: What does @Transactional do, and when does Spring roll a transaction back?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @Transactional runs a method inside one database transaction; it commits on success and rolls back on unchecked exceptions. It only works through Spring's proxy, so it needs a public method called from another bean.
tips: Lead with the money-transfer example — atomicity is easiest to explain with it.
Name the self-invocation trap: it is the most asked @Transactional follow-up.
interviewQuestions.title: @Transactional basics

commonMistakes: Saying a unique key cannot be null — it can, in most databases, and MySQL even allows several nulls in one.
Putting two primary keys on one table instead of one composite primary key.
Choosing a natural key (like an email) as the primary key when it can change — a surrogate id is usually safer.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Both enforce uniqueness, but they differ in three ways. A table can have only one primary key, and it can never contain null; a table can have many unique keys, and a unique column can usually contain null (MySQL allows multiple nulls in a unique column). A primary key identifies each row — it is the table's identity — while a unique key is an extra rule saying 'this value must not repeat'.

In practice: give every table a primary key (usually an auto-increment id), and add unique keys for business values that must be one-per-row, such as an email address. In MySQL's InnoDB, the primary key also decides how rows are physically stored (the clustered index), so lookups by primary key are the fastest access path, while unique keys get a secondary index.

```sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL
);
```
followUps: Can a primary key be made of more than one column?
What is a foreign key, and how is it different from a unique key?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a primary key and a unique key?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: One primary key per table, never null, identifies each row; many unique keys allowed, usually nullable, enforcing no repeats on a business value like an email.
tips: Give the three differences as a list: count, nulls, purpose.
Mention the InnoDB clustered-index point — it shows you know why the primary key matters for performance.
interviewQuestions.title: Primary key vs unique key

commonMistakes: Using HAVING without GROUP BY to filter rows — that is WHERE's job.
Putting an aggregate condition in WHERE, which fails because WHERE runs before grouping.
Forgetting that WHERE cannot see column aliases defined in the SELECT list in most databases.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY has run. That ordering decides what each clause can express: WHERE can test plain columns but not aggregates, while HAVING can test aggregates such as AVG(salary) > 50000 but cannot cheaply test individual rows.

```sql
SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE status = 'active'
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000;
```

Here WHERE first drops inactive employees, then GROUP BY forms one group per department, then HAVING keeps only departments whose average salary is above 50,000. A quick way to remember it: WHERE is a row filter, HAVING is a group filter — and any condition that mentions an aggregate function belongs in HAVING.
followUps: Can you use HAVING without GROUP BY?
Why does putting AVG(salary) > 50000 in the WHERE clause fail?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can test aggregates like AVG(salary).
tips: Walk through one query showing both clauses in order — it proves you know the execution sequence.
Use the memory hook: WHERE is a row filter, HAVING is a group filter.
interviewQuestions.title: WHERE vs HAVING

commonMistakes: Letting every client call services directly and duplicating auth, rate limiting, and routing in each client.
Treating the gateway as the place for business logic — it should route and protect, not implement features.
Forgetting the gateway is a single point of failure unless it is itself deployed redundantly.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
An API Gateway is the single front door for all client traffic. Instead of clients calling dozens of services directly, they call the gateway, which routes each request to the right service, and handles the jobs that are the same for every service: authentication, rate limiting, request logging, CORS, and sometimes response aggregation (combining calls to several services into one response for a mobile client).

That centralisation is the benefit and the risk. It simplifies clients — one base URL, one auth flow — and lets teams change a service's address or version without touching every client. But the gateway is now on the critical path for everything, so it must be fast, stateless, and run with several instances behind a load balancer; if it goes down, every service becomes unreachable even though the services themselves are healthy.
followUps: What is the difference between an API Gateway and a service registry?
How does a gateway differ from a load balancer?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the role of an API Gateway in a microservices architecture?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The gateway is the single entry point: it routes requests to the right service and centralises auth, rate limiting, and logging — but it must be redundant, since it is on the critical path.
tips: List the cross-cutting jobs (auth, rate limiting, logging) — that is what the gateway is for.
Name the trade-off in the same breath: single point of failure unless deployed redundantly.
interviewQuestions.title: API Gateway in microservices

commonMistakes: Running mvn install when you only meant to compile — it runs tests, packages, and writes to the local repository.
Using -DskipTests when you meant -Dmaven.test.skip: skipTests still compiles tests, maven.test.skip skips compiling them too.
Deleting the target folder by hand instead of running mvn clean, which is the repeatable way to get a fresh build.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Maven builds run through lifecycle phases in a fixed order: validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy. Running mvn install executes every phase up to install: it compiles the code, runs the tests, packages the jar, and copies it into your local repository (~/.m2) so other local projects can use it. Running mvn clean first deletes the target directory, so nothing stale survives from the previous build — mvn clean install is the standard 'fresh build' command.

In this scenario, start by reading the failure, not re-running blindly. If a test fails, the build stops at the test phase and later phases never run — that is by design. Fix the failing test or the code it caught; only skip tests deliberately with -DskipTests (tests are compiled but not run) when you need a package urgently and understand the risk, and never skip them in CI. If the failure is a missing dependency, check the pom.xml: a dependency declared with the wrong scope (for example, test scope on a library used in main code) compiles in one place and fails in another. And if the build works for a teammate but not for you, delete target with mvn clean and check for a stale artifact in your local repository.
followUps: What is the difference between mvn package and mvn install?
What does -DskipTests do differently from -Dmaven.test.skip?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: your teammate's Maven build works, but yours fails — and a full mvn clean install is the first thing you are told to run. What does that command actually do, and how do you diagnose the failure?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: mvn clean install deletes target, then runs every phase up to install (compile, test, package, install to ~/.m2). A test failure stops the build by design — read the failure, fix the cause, and only skip tests deliberately.
tips: Recite the phase order — validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy.
Name the two skip flags and their difference; it is the classic follow-up.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: diagnosing a failing Maven build

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Checked exceptions must be declared or handled, and they are meant for recoverable conditions such as a missing file or a failed network call, while unchecked exceptions usually signal programming errors such as a null dereference or an illegal argument. Overusing checked exceptions leaks implementation details through every caller, so many modern codebases wrap them in a meaningful unchecked exception at a boundary. Try-with-resources guarantees that each resource is closed in reverse order of opening, even when an exception occurs, and any exception thrown during close is added as a suppressed exception rather than hiding the original failure. Always close resources you open, log the original exception with context, and avoid catching Exception just to swallow it.
followUps: When would you wrap a checked exception instead of declaring it?
How do you inspect a suppressed exception?
interviewQuestions.question: When should you use a checked exception versus an unchecked exception, and how does try-with-resources change exception handling?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Checked for recoverable conditions, unchecked for programming errors; try-with-resources closes resources reliably and preserves the original exception, adding close failures as suppressed exceptions.
tips: Name a concrete recoverable case and a concrete programming-error case.
Mention suppressed exceptions — it shows you have debugged real resource code.
interviewQuestions.title: Checked vs unchecked exceptions

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: HashMap is not thread-safe and its iterators are fail-fast, so a concurrent modification during iteration usually throws ConcurrentModificationException, whereas ConcurrentHashMap iterators are weakly consistent and tolerate concurrent updates without throwing. ConcurrentHashMap also forbids null keys and null values, because a null return from get would be ambiguous when another thread could have removed the entry. Its atomic methods such as computeIfAbsent, merge, and putIfAbsent let you update a shared map without external locking, but the mapping function must be short and side-effect free, since it may be retried. For counters or grouped results, combine it with atomic values such as LongAdder or a concurrent collection rather than synchronizing the whole map.
followUps: Why does ConcurrentHashMap forbid null keys and values?
When is computeIfAbsent unsafe?
interviewQuestions.question: How does ConcurrentHashMap differ from a synchronized HashMap, and when would you choose it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: ConcurrentHashMap is lock-striped, thread-safe, weakly consistent for iteration, and forbids nulls; a synchronized HashMap serializes all access and still fails fast on concurrent iteration.
tips: Contrast fail-fast with weakly consistent iteration explicitly.
Warn that computeIfAbsent functions must be short and side-effect free.
interviewQuestions.title: ConcurrentHashMap vs synchronized HashMap

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Parallel streams split work across the common ForkJoinPool, which helps only for large, CPU-bound, splittable workloads with independent, non-blocking operations. They hurt when the source is small, the work is I/O-bound, the operations block, or the pipeline uses stateful operations such as sorted or distinct that force coordination, and they can starve other tasks sharing the common pool. Stateful lambda side effects, such as appending to a shared list, break correctness in parallel pipelines, so collect results with a proper collector instead. A good answer names the workload, checks its size, avoids blocking calls, and measures before and after rather than assuming parallelism is faster.
followUps: Why should you not do blocking I/O inside a parallel stream?
How do you collect results safely from a parallel stream?
interviewQuestions.question: When does a parallel stream help, and when does it make performance worse?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Parallel streams help only for large CPU-bound work over a splittable source; they hurt for small, blocking, or I/O-bound work and can starve the shared common pool.
tips: Give the three conditions: large, CPU-bound, splittable.
Mention that the common ForkJoinPool is shared, so a slow stream affects the whole application.
interviewQuestions.title: Parallel streams: help or harm

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: CompletableFuture chains such as thenApply, thenCompose, and thenCombine let you express dependent and independent async steps without blocking, while exceptionally and handle let you recover or translate failures at a defined point in the chain. The most common production failure is submitting many futures to an unbounded or too-small pool, so dependent stages queue up and the whole pipeline stalls even though no thread has deadlocked. Always supply an explicit executor for blocking or long-running stages, bound the pool and its queue, set timeouts with orTimeout, and decide where exceptions are observed, because an unobserved future failure is silently lost. For fan-out work, combine futures with allOf and then inspect each result individually rather than assuming success.
followUps: What happens when a CompletableFuture exception is never observed?
Why should blocking stages not use the common ForkJoinPool?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you chain CompletableFuture stages safely in production, and what usually goes wrong?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Chain with thenApply, thenCompose, and thenCombine, handle failures explicitly, use a dedicated bounded executor for blocking stages, and apply timeouts.
tips: Name the thread-pool exhaustion failure mode, not just the API methods.
Mention orTimeout and explicit exception handling in the same answer.
interviewQuestions.title: CompletableFuture in production

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Most modern collectors divide the heap into young and old generations, because most objects die young: short-lived objects are collected cheaply in the young generation, while survivors are promoted to the old generation, which is collected less often but more expensively. G1 divides the heap into regions and targets a pause-time goal by collecting the regions with the most garbage first, whereas the Parallel collector prioritizes throughput and accepts longer pauses. Frequent full garbage collections, long promotion failures, or a steadily growing old generation usually point to a leak, an undersized heap, or objects that live longer than expected. Tune by measuring pause times and allocation rates first, then adjust heap size and collector choice, rather than guessing flags.
followUps: How do you tell a leak apart from a heap that is simply too small?
When would you prefer throughput over low pause time?
interviewQuestions.question: How do generational garbage collectors work, and how do you choose between G1 and Parallel GC?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Young objects are collected cheaply and survivors are promoted; G1 targets pause time with region-based collection, Parallel targets throughput with longer pauses.
tips: Explain the generational hypothesis before naming collectors.
Tie the choice to a measurable goal: pause time versus throughput.
interviewQuestions.title: Generational GC and collector choice

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Singleton is the default scope, so the container creates one instance per application context, while prototype creates a new instance on every request for the bean. The classic trap is injecting a prototype bean into a singleton: the injection happens once, so the singleton keeps the same prototype instance forever. Fix it by injecting a provider, such as ObjectProvider or Provider, and asking for a fresh instance on each use, or by using a scoped proxy. Request and session scopes only exist in a web context, and relying on them in a service layer makes the service untestable outside a request, so keep scope decisions at the edge where they belong.
followUps: How do you get a fresh prototype instance inside a singleton?
Why is request scope a poor fit for a service bean?
interviewQuestions.question: What goes wrong when a prototype bean is injected into a singleton, and how do you fix it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The singleton captures one prototype instance at injection time; inject ObjectProvider or Provider and request a fresh instance per use, or use a scoped proxy.
tips: State the trap first, then the fix — interviewers want both.
Mention that prototype beans are not destroyed by the container.
interviewQuestions.title: Prototype beans in singletons

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Spring Boot resolves configuration from many sources in a defined precedence order, roughly: command-line arguments and environment variables beat application properties files, which beat packaged defaults, and profile-specific files such as application-prod.properties beat the base application.properties within the same source type. Binding properties into a validated @ConfigurationProperties class is safer than scattering @Value annotations, because it groups related settings, supports relaxed binding and type conversion, and fails fast on invalid values when validation is enabled. Secrets should come from environment variables or a secret store, never from a committed properties file, and profile-specific behaviour should be expressed as configuration, not as if-statements scattered through code. When a value surprises you, check the active profiles and the effective property source order before assuming the code is wrong.
followUps: Where should secrets live, and why not in application.properties?
How do you fail fast on invalid configuration?
interviewQuestions.question: How does Spring Boot decide which configuration value wins, and how should you structure configuration for multiple environments?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Higher-precedence sources such as command-line arguments and environment variables beat properties files, and profile-specific files beat the base file; bind settings into validated @ConfigurationProperties classes.
tips: Recite the precedence order in one sentence.
Recommend @ConfigurationProperties over scattered @Value.
interviewQuestions.title: Profiles and configuration precedence

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A @RestControllerAdvice class centralizes exception handling across controllers, mapping each exception type to a consistent error body and HTTP status, so controllers stay focused on happy-path logic. Bean Validation annotations such as @NotNull, @Size, and @Pattern on a request DTO, triggered by @Valid, reject bad input before business logic runs, and validation failures arrive as a MethodArgumentNotValidException you can translate in the same advice class. Return ResponseEntity when the status or headers vary, such as 201 Created with a Location header after creating a resource, and keep error bodies stable with fields for a code, a message, and request context. Never leak stack traces or internal exception messages to clients, and never use exceptions for ordinary control flow.
followUps: Where does validation run relative to controller logic?
What should a stable API error body contain?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you design consistent error handling and validation for a Spring MVC REST API?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Validate DTOs with Bean Validation, translate exceptions centrally in @RestControllerAdvice into stable error bodies, and use ResponseEntity when status or headers vary.
tips: Pair validation and exception translation — they belong together in the answer.
Mention 201 with a Location header as the ResponseEntity example.
interviewQuestions.title: REST error handling and validation

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Derived query methods are readable for simple lookups, but they grow unwieldy for complex conditions, so use @Query for explicit JPQL or native SQL, and projections or DTO queries when you only need a few columns. Pagination with Pageable is convenient, but offset pagination degrades on large tables because the database still scans skipped rows, so keyset pagination on an ordered unique key is better for infinite-scroll or export workloads. Keep transaction boundaries at the service layer, not the repository, so a unit of work that touches several repositories commits or rolls back together, and avoid lazy-loading collections inside a controller after the transaction has closed.
