The practical difference for diagnosis is that a growing heap points to retained objects, while a growing Metaspace points to classes being loaded and never unloaded, usually because a classloader is held by a static reference, a thread-local, or a registered driver or listener. Setting a cap is worth doing in production: without one, a classloader leak consumes native memory until the whole process is killed, and with one, it fails fast with a clear Metaspace error instead.
followUps: Why can a class only be unloaded when its classloader is unreachable?
What is a sensible MaxMetaspaceSize for a service, and why set one at all?
How do repeated redeploys in the same JVM cause Metaspace growth?
interviewQuestions.question: What is Metaspace, how does it differ from PermGen, and what does Metaspace growth tell you in production?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Metaspace replaced PermGen in Java 8 and holds class metadata in native memory with a default limit that grows as needed, so steady Metaspace growth usually points to a classloader leak rather than a heap leak.
tips: Contrast the failure mode: PermGen failed fast, Metaspace grows silently.
Tie the diagnosis to classloaders, not to heap dumps.
interviewQuestions.title: Metaspace versus PermGen

commonMistakes: Reading fields in a different order than they were written.
Forgetting the public no-arg constructor and getting an InvalidClassException.
Using Externalizable when plain Serializable with transient fields would do.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: With Serializable, the JVM uses reflection to write the object's fields for you, which is easy but gives you no say over the format, the size, or which fields are included beyond marking fields transient. Externalizable extends Serializable and requires a public no-arg constructor plus readExternal and writeExternal methods that you write yourself, so you decide the exact bytes, the order, and how to handle fields added in a later version. That control is useful when the default format is too large, when you need a stable wire format across versions, or when some fields need custom handling such as encryption. The price is that you must keep the read and write order in step yourself, and forgetting a field or reading in the wrong order corrupts the stream silently. For most application code, Serializable plus a serialVersionUID and a few transient fields is enough; reach for Externalizable when the serialized form itself is part of your contract.
followUps: Why does Externalizable require a public no-arg constructor?
What goes wrong if readExternal reads fields in a different order than writeExternal wrote them?
How would you keep a serialized form compatible when you add a field?
interviewQuestions.question: How does Externalizable differ from Serializable, and when would you choose one over the other?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Serializable lets the JVM write every non-transient field automatically; Externalizable hands full control to your readExternal and writeExternal methods, so you choose exactly what is written and in what order.
tips: Frame it as control versus convenience.
Mention the no-arg constructor requirement; interviewers listen for it.
interviewQuestions.title: Externalizable versus Serializable

commonMistakes: Assuming loadClass runs static initialisers.
Breaking parent delegation and loading two copies of the same class.
Keeping a reference to a classloader and wondering why its classes never unload.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A JVM has three built-in loaders in a parent chain: the bootstrap loader loads the core JDK classes, the platform loader loads platform modules, and the application loader loads classes from the classpath. A custom loader, such as the one a web container creates per application, sits below these. Loading follows parent delegation: a loader asks its parent first and only loads the class itself if no parent can, which is what stops an application from replacing a core class like java.lang.String with its own version. Class.forName() loads the class and runs its static initialisers immediately, which is why it is used to trigger driver registration; ClassLoader.loadClass() only loads and links the class, and its static block runs later when the class is first used. That difference matters when a static block has side effects or when you want to inspect a class without running its initialisation. Classes are only unloaded when their loader becomes unreachable, which is why a leaked loader keeps every class it loaded alive in Metaspace.
followUps: Why does parent delegation stop an application replacing java.lang.String?
When would you create a custom classloader, and what breaks if you skip delegation?
Why does a leaked classloader show up as Metaspace growth?
interviewQuestions.question: What are the classloaders in a JVM, how does delegation work, and how do Class.forName() and ClassLoader.loadClass() differ?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Bootstrap, platform, and application loaders delegate upwards before loading a class themselves; forName loads and initialises the class, while loadClass only loads it and leaves static initialisation for later.
tips: Draw the three loaders as a chain before explaining delegation.
State the forName versus loadClass difference as initialise now versus initialise later.
interviewQuestions.title: Classloaders: types, delegation, and loading a class

commonMistakes: Returning a shallow copy and letting callers mutate shared state.
Forgetting to make clone public or to handle CloneNotSupportedException.
Deep-copying immutable fields such as Strings for no benefit.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A shallow copy creates a new object and copies each field value across, so a field that points to a list or another object still points to the same list or object in both copies; changing it through one copy changes it for the other. A deep copy also copies every referenced object, so the two graphs are fully independent, which is what you want when the copy must be safe to mutate on its own. Java's built-in route is awkward: Cloneable is only a marker interface, Object.clone() is protected and throws CloneNotSupportedException, and the default implementation is shallow, so you must override clone, make it public, handle the exception, and manually deep-copy each mutable field yourself. For that reason, most teams prefer a copy constructor or a small factory method that builds a new object field by field: the intent is visible, the depth is explicit, and there is no checked exception or protected method to work around. Whichever route you take, document whether the copy is deep or shallow, because callers will assume one or the other.
followUps: When is a shallow copy actually safe to hand out?
How would you deep-copy an object graph without writing clone at all?
Why do many teams avoid Cloneable in favour of a copy constructor?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between deep and shallow cloning, and what are the traps in Java's Cloneable design?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A shallow copy duplicates the object but shares its referenced fields; a deep copy duplicates those fields too. Cloneable is a marker interface with a protected, exception-throwing clone method, so it is easy to get wrong.
tips: Give one shared-reference example that shows the shallow-copy trap.
State your preference and why, rather than only describing clone().
interviewQuestions.title: Deep versus shallow cloning

commonMistakes: Checking the condition with if instead of while.
Calling wait or notify outside a synchronized block.
Using notify and waking a thread waiting on the wrong condition.
followUps: What goes wrong if you use notify() instead of notifyAll() here?
Why must wait() be called while holding the monitor?
When would you replace this with a BlockingQueue, and what do you lose?
interviewQuestions.question: Coding task: write a bounded producer-consumer buffer in plain Java using wait() and notifyAll(). Why must the condition be checked in a while loop, not an if?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Guard the buffer with synchronized methods, wait in a while loop when it is full or empty, and notifyAll after each change; the while loop protects against spurious wakeups and against another thread taking the item first.
tips: Write the while loop first and explain it before the rest.
Mention spurious wakeups by name.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: producer-consumer with wait and notify

commonMistakes: Capturing an argument when the expected object was already known.
Verifying every interaction instead of the one that defines the behaviour.
Stubbing with any() and then asserting nothing about the values.
followUps: When is a plain verify with an expected object better than a captor?
How does verifyNoMoreInteractions differ from verify with times(1)?
Why is stubbing a mock you then verify a smell?
interviewQuestions.question: Coding task: how do you test that a service saves exactly the right entity using Mockito, and when do you reach for an ArgumentCaptor instead of a simple verify?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Stub the dependencies, call the service, then verify the repository method was called once and capture its argument to assert on the saved fields; use a captor when the exact argument is built inside the method and you cannot construct it in advance.
tips: Explain the trigger first: the argument is built inside the method.
Keep one behaviour per test.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: verify behaviour with Mockito ArgumentCaptor

commonMistakes: Forgetting readResolve and creating a second instance on deserialization.
Thinking a private constructor alone makes a Singleton safe.
Using a Singleton for mutable global state that tests cannot reset.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A classic Singleton with a private constructor and a static instance looks safe, but it has three holes. Reflection can make the private constructor accessible and call it, producing a second instance; deserialization creates a new object without calling the constructor, so reading a serialized Singleton back gives you a second instance unless you add a readResolve method that returns the existing one; and cloning copies the instance unless clone is blocked. The usual defences are to throw from the constructor if an instance already exists, which stops reflection, to add readResolve, which stops deserialization, and to refuse cloning. The simpler and stronger answer is an enum with a single constant: the JVM guarantees one instance per classloader, serialization is handled by the language, and reflection cannot instantiate an enum, so all three attacks fail by construction. The trade-off is that an enum cannot extend another class and is awkward when construction needs parameters, in which case a static holder class with lazy initialisation plus the defences above is the fallback.
followUps: Why does readResolve fix the deserialization hole?
What breaks if you serialize a Singleton without readResolve?
When would you avoid a Singleton entirely, even a safe one?
interviewQuestions.question: How can a Singleton be broken in Java, and what is the most robust way to implement one?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Reflection can call the private constructor, deserialization can create a second instance, and cloning can copy it; an enum singleton is immune to all three, which is why it is the most robust form.
tips: Name all three attacks, then give the enum answer.
Mention that enum singletons cannot extend a class.
interviewQuestions.title: How a Singleton breaks, and how to defend it

commonMistakes: Using an Abstract Factory for a single product type.
Letting callers mix products from different families.
Putting creation logic in the caller and calling it a factory.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Factory Method solves the problem of creating a single product: a creator class defines a method that returns a product, and each subclass decides which concrete product to build, so the calling code depends only on the product interface. Abstract Factory solves a bigger problem: creating a family of related products that belong together, such as a button, a text field, and a scroll bar that must all follow the same visual theme. It defines one factory interface with a creation method per product, and each concrete factory produces the whole matching set, so a caller cannot accidentally mix a dark-theme button with a light-theme text field. Choose Factory Method when you have one product type and the variation is which implementation is built; choose Abstract Factory when you have several related types and the variation is which consistent family is built. In Spring, a @Bean factory method is the everyday form of the first idea, while choosing between whole configuration families is the second idea in framework form.
followUps: What breaks if you mix products from two Abstract Factory families?
How does a Spring @Bean method relate to the Factory Method idea?
Why is the factory itself usually hidden behind an interface?
interviewQuestions.question: How do the Factory Method and Abstract Factory patterns differ, and how do you choose between them?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Factory Method creates one kind of object and lets subclasses decide the concrete type; Abstract Factory creates a whole family of related objects that must work together, such as a matching set of UI controls.
tips: Use one product versus a family of products as the dividing line.
Give a concrete family example, such as a UI theme.
interviewQuestions.title: Factory versus Abstract Factory

commonMistakes: Adding a builder to a two-field class.
Validating each field alone and missing invalid combinations.
Exposing the half-built object before build() is called.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A constructor with many parameters is hard to call correctly: callers mix up two Strings or two ints, and adding an optional field forces either a new constructor or a null argument. Telescoping constructors, where each constructor adds one more parameter, multiply quickly and still leave the caller guessing which argument is which. A builder fixes this by giving each field a named setter-like step, letting optional fields be left out, and producing an immutable object at the end through a single build step that can validate the whole combination. The cost is a second class, more code to maintain, and an object that is mutable during construction, so a builder is overkill for a small value object with two or three required fields, where a constructor or a record is simpler and clearer. In interviews, the honest answer names the threshold: roughly four or more parameters, or any case where two parameters share a type and could be swapped by mistake.
followUps: How does a builder help make an immutable object?
Where would you validate: in each builder step or in build()?
Why is a record sometimes a better answer than a builder?
interviewQuestions.question: When is the Builder pattern the right choice over constructors, and when does it become overkill?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use a builder when an object has many parameters, several optional ones, or combinations that would need many constructors; skip it for small objects with two or three required fields, where a plain constructor is clearer.
tips: Name the threshold: four or more parameters, or same-type parameters that can be swapped.
Mention validation in build() as the place to check the whole combination.
interviewQuestions.title: Builder versus telescoping constructors

commonMistakes: Listing patterns without a Spring example for any of them.
Confusing a container-managed singleton bean with a hand-written Singleton class.
Calling every @Bean method a factory without explaining what it creates.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Spring is a good place to show pattern knowledge because the framework uses the patterns rather than just describing them. The IoC container is a factory: you ask for a bean by name or type and it decides which concrete class to build. Beans are singletons by default, with the container holding one shared instance per scope. AOP and @Transactional are proxies: the container wraps your bean so cross-cutting behaviour runs around your method. JdbcTemplate and RestTemplate are template methods: the framework owns the fixed steps, such as opening and closing resources, and you supply only the varying part. Adapters appear wherever Spring bridges two APIs, for example HandlerAdapter letting one dispatcher call controllers written in different styles. Naming the pattern is only half the answer; the senior version points at the concrete class or annotation in your own project and explains what would break if the pattern were removed.
followUps: Why are Spring singleton beans not the same as a Singleton pattern class?
How does a proxy change what happens when one bean method calls another?
Where does the Observer pattern appear in Spring?
interviewQuestions.question: Which design patterns does the Spring Framework itself use, and where can you point to each one in real code?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Spring is built on patterns: the container is a factory, beans are singletons by default, proxies add advice, templates handle boilerplate, and adapters bridge different APIs.
tips: Give the pattern and the Spring class together, not the pattern alone.
Use the proxy example to connect back to @Transactional behaviour.
interviewQuestions.title: Design patterns inside the Spring Framework

commonMistakes: Calling an @Async method from the same bean and expecting it to run in the background.
Using the default executor under load.
Letting exceptions from void @Async methods vanish silently.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Marking a method @Async and enabling async support makes Spring run it through a proxy on a thread from a TaskExecutor instead of the caller's thread, returning a Future or CompletableFuture you can compose. The default executor is a simple one that creates a new thread per task, so a production setup should define its own ThreadPoolTaskExecutor with a bounded queue, a named thread prefix, and a rejection policy, otherwise a burst of async calls can exhaust threads exactly like any other unbounded pool. The trap is the same proxy rule as @Transactional: the proxy only intercepts calls that arrive from outside the bean, so when one method of a bean calls its own @Async method, the call never reaches the proxy and the work runs synchronously on the caller's thread with no error to warn you. The fixes are the same too: call the async method through another bean, or inject the bean's own proxy. Exceptions also need care: a void @Async method that throws has no caller to receive the exception, so configure an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler to log it, or return a CompletableFuture so failures can be handled.
followUps: Why does a self-call run synchronously instead of failing loudly?
What should a production TaskExecutor configure that the default does not?
Where does a thrown exception go from a void @Async method?
interviewQuestions.question: How does @Async work in Spring, what executor does it need, and what goes wrong when an @Async method is called from the same bean?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @Async runs the method on a separate thread through a proxy, so it needs a configured TaskExecutor and an external call; a self-call bypasses the proxy and runs synchronously on the caller's thread.
tips: Connect the trap to the proxy rule, not to async itself.
Name the executor configuration as a production requirement.
interviewQuestions.title: @Async, executors, and the self-invocation trap

commonMistakes: Creating beans unconditionally so consumers cannot override them.
Forgetting the properties prefix so settings collide with other starters.
Bundling a heavy dependency every consumer is forced to carry.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A custom starter has two parts: a small module that declares the dependencies a team always needs together, and an auto-configuration class that creates the beans for that setup. The auto-configuration is registered so Spring Boot can find it, and it is guarded by conditions: @ConditionalOnClass so it only applies when the library is present, @ConditionalOnMissingBean so a team's own bean wins, and @ConditionalOnProperty so the whole setup can be switched off. Configuration properties bind the team's settings from application properties with a clear prefix, and the starter should be ordered after the auto-configurations it depends on. The value for consumers is that a new service gets logging, metrics, security defaults, or client setup by adding one dependency instead of copying the same configuration class into every project. The risks to name are a starter that is too opinionated and hard to override, and a starter that drags in a heavy dependency every consumer must then exclude.
followUps: How does a team's own bean override a starter's bean?
How do you let a team switch a starter off without removing the dependency?
What makes a starter too opinionated to reuse?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you build a custom Spring Boot starter, and what does auto-configuration do for the teams that use it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A starter is a dependency that pulls in the libraries a team needs, plus an auto-configuration class that creates the beans only when its conditions match, so consumers get a working setup by adding one dependency.
tips: Describe the two parts first: dependency plus auto-configuration.
Name the three conditions as the mechanism that makes it safe.
interviewQuestions.title: Building a custom Spring Boot starter

commonMistakes: Assuming one @Transactional covers both databases.
Leaking the tenant key in a ThreadLocal across requests.
Forgetting @Primary and getting an ambiguous-bean failure at startup.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Spring Boot auto-configures a single DataSource, so a second database needs explicit beans: one DataSource, one EntityManagerFactory, and one transaction manager per database, with one of each marked @Primary so injection still works where only one is needed. To choose at runtime, for example per tenant, use AbstractRoutingDataSource, which picks the target DataSource from a key held in a ThreadLocal context that is set early in the request, usually by a filter or interceptor, and cleared afterwards so the thread does not leak the tenant into the next request. The hard part is transactions: a @Transactional method uses one transaction manager, so a write that touches both databases is two separate transactions and can commit in one and fail in the other. The honest answer is to avoid spanning databases in one transaction: keep each operation to one source, or accept eventual consistency with a saga or outbox. Also name the testing cost: each DataSource doubles the test setup, and a forgotten @Primary produces an ambiguous-bean error at startup.
followUps: Why must the routing key be cleared after the request?
What happens if you forget @Primary with two DataSources?
How would you handle a write that must touch both databases?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you configure multiple DataSources in Spring Boot, switch between them at runtime, and what breaks with transactions?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Define one DataSource bean per database, mark one @Primary, and route with AbstractRoutingDataSource driven by a context holder; transactions spanning both databases are not atomic, so keep each transaction to one source or use a saga.
tips: List the three beans per database before the routing part.
State plainly that cross-database transactions are not atomic.
interviewQuestions.title: Multiple DataSources and runtime routing

commonMistakes: Adding instances before checking whether the database is the bottleneck.
Raising the connection pool without checking what the database can handle.
Scaling a stateful service and splitting user sessions across instances.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start by finding the real bottleneck instead of guessing: check CPU, memory, thread-pool queue depth, database connection pool usage, and the slowest endpoints, and look at whether latency comes from the service, the database, or a downstream call. If the service itself is stateless, the fastest safe move is to add instances behind the load balancer, since a stateless service scales horizontally without code changes. Next protect the shared resources: raise the database connection pool only as far as the database can handle, add caching for hot read endpoints, and add timeouts and circuit breakers on downstream calls so a slow dependency cannot exhaust your threads. Then look at the code: add indexes for the slow queries, move heavy work off the request thread with async processing or a queue, and check for accidental per-request work such as repeated serialization or uncached lookups. Finally, make sure the change is safe to run: confirm sessions are not stored in memory on one instance, confirm the deployment can roll out without downtime, and set alerts on the metrics you just watched so the next doubling is caught earlier.
followUps: How do you know whether the bottleneck is the service or the database?
Why can raising the connection pool make things worse?
What breaks if the service keeps session state in memory?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: your Spring Boot service must suddenly handle twice the traffic it was designed for. What do you do first, and what do you change next?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: First confirm where the bottleneck is with metrics and logs, then scale out behind a load balancer and protect the database with pooling, caching, and timeouts; only then tune the code, because scaling a bottleneck just moves it.
tips: Order the answer: measure, scale out, protect shared resources, then tune code.
Name one metric for each layer.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: doubling traffic on a Spring Boot service

commonMistakes: Adding an index without reading the plan first.
Testing the fix on a tiny dataset.
Fixing the query while the real problem is N+1 in the application.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start with the execution plan: EXPLAIN shows whether the database uses an index or scans the whole table, how many rows it expects to touch, and whether it sorts or joins in an expensive order. The usual causes are a missing index on the filtered or joined column, a query that defeats its index with a function on the column or a leading wildcard, a table that has grown past the point where the old plan works, or stale statistics that make the planner choose badly. Fixes follow the cause: add a covering index for the columns the query actually reads, rewrite the query so the filter can use the index, or update statistics and re-check the plan. Measure on realistic data volumes, because a query that is fast on a thousand rows can be slow on ten million, and check the fix under the same load, since an index that helps one query slows every write to the table. Also check the application side: an N+1 pattern, where one query per row replaces one joined query, often looks like a slow query but is really a slow loop.
followUps: How do you tell a missing index from stale statistics?
Why can an index that fixes a read hurt overall performance?
When is the real problem N+1 rather than the query itself?
interviewQuestions.question: A query that was fast is now slow in production. How do you find the cause and fix it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Run EXPLAIN to see the plan, check whether an index is used and how many rows are scanned, then fix the query or the index, and verify the plan changed on production-like data volumes.
tips: Start every answer with EXPLAIN.
Tie each cause to its fix.
interviewQuestions.title: Diagnosing a slow query in production

commonMistakes: Adding a filter without a position and letting it land in a random spot.
Doing heavy work in a filter that runs on every request.
Assuming filters only run for controller requests.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Every request passes through a chain of servlet filters before it reaches a controller, and Spring Security owns that chain: one filter checks the security context, another handles login, another checks the user's roles against the URL, and another writes the security context back at the end. A custom filter, such as one that reads a token from a header and builds an authentication object, is added in the security configuration with addFilterBefore or addFilterAfter, positioned relative to a filter whose job you understand, for example before the filter that checks authorization, so your authentication is in place when the check runs. Putting it in the wrong place is the classic bug: after the authorization check it never runs in time, and before the context filter it cannot rely on the security context existing. Filters are servlet-level, so they run for every request including errors and static resources, and they should do one small job and pass the request on quickly; heavy work in a filter slows every request. For debugging, enable security debug logging to see which filter rejected a request and why.
followUps: What happens if your filter runs after the authorization filter?
Why should a filter do only one small job?
How do you find out which filter rejected a request?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the Spring Security filter chain, how do you add a custom filter, and where does it belong in the order?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Security is a chain of servlet filters that runs before your controllers; a custom filter is added with addFilterBefore or addFilterAfter relative to a known filter, and its position decides what it can see and what it can break.
tips: Explain position as the whole answer: before or after a known filter.
Name the classic bug: the filter runs too late.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring Security filter chain and custom filters

commonMistakes: Adding consumers beyond the partition count and expecting more throughput.
Ignoring rebalances as a cause of lag.
Assuming replication alone prevents data loss.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Consumer lag is the gap between the newest message and the last one a group has processed, and it is measured per partition, so the first step is to see whether one partition is stuck or all of them are behind. Common causes are slow processing in the consumer, too few consumers for the partition count, since a partition can only be read by one consumer in a group, and frequent rebalances, where a consumer joining or leaving stops the whole group while partitions are reassigned. Rebalances get slow when consumers take long to finish their current work or hold large state, and the fix is usually a mix of faster processing, more partitions, and the cooperative rebalancing protocol that moves fewer partitions at a time. When a partition leader fails, the cluster elects a new leader from the in-sync replicas, and consumers resume from there; the risk is the window where the leader accepted a write that no replica had copied yet, in which case that write is lost even though replication was configured. To shrink that window, require the producer to wait for all in-sync replicas before acknowledging, and keep the minimum in-sync replica count above one so a single replica cannot accept writes alone.
followUps: Why can a group not scale past its partition count?
What makes a rebalance slow, and what does cooperative rebalancing change?
How can data be lost even with replication enabled?
interviewQuestions.question: Your Kafka consumers are falling behind and rebalances take a long time. How do you diagnose it, and what happens when a partition leader fails?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Check lag per partition, slow processing, and rebalance causes first; add consumers up to the partition count or speed up processing, and remember a failed leader is replaced by an in-sync replica, but data can still be lost if the leader dies before replicas catch up.
tips: Start with lag per partition, not total lag.
Name the lost-write window explicitly.
interviewQuestions.title: Kafka consumer lag, rebalances, and broker failure

commonMistakes: Letting a choreographed saga grow until nobody can trace it.
Writing a compensating action that cannot safely run twice.
Treating a compensation as a database rollback.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A saga breaks a multi-service transaction into local steps, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails. Choreography runs the saga without a boss: each service listens for an event, does its step, and publishes the next event, so the flow is defined by the services themselves. That is simple and loosely coupled for a short chain, but the overall flow is invisible: no one place shows the order, a missing event is hard to spot, and adding a step means changing several services. Orchestration puts one coordinator in charge: it calls each service in order, tracks which steps have completed, and runs the compensations in reverse when one fails. That makes the flow visible, testable, and easy to change, at the cost of a central service that every step depends on. Choose choreography when the flow is short, stable, and each service owns its part; choose orchestration when the flow is long, branches on results, or needs a clear audit trail. Either way, compensations must be idempotent, because a retry can run one twice, and every participant must handle duplicate events.
followUps: What breaks first when a choreographed saga grows to ten steps?
How does the orchestrator know which compensations to run after a failure?
Why must a compensating action be idempotent?
interviewQuestions.question: How do choreography and orchestration differ as ways to run a saga, and how do you choose between them?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: In choreography each service reacts to events on its own; in orchestration one coordinator tells each service what to do. Choreography is looser and simpler for short flows, orchestration is clearer and easier to debug for long, branching flows.
tips: Contrast who holds the flow: nobody, or one coordinator.
Give the decision rule as flow length and branching.
interviewQuestions.title: Saga choreography versus orchestration

commonMistakes: Sharing one pool across all dependencies and calling it a bulkhead.
Sizing pools by guesswork instead of latency and traffic.
Queueing rejected calls instead of failing fast.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The pattern is named after a ship: watertight compartments keep one leak from sinking the whole vessel. In a service, the compartments are resource pools: each downstream dependency gets its own thread pool, its own database connection pool, or a semaphore limiting concurrent calls, so a slow payment service can exhaust only its own pool while the rest of the service keeps answering. In Spring Boot the usual implementation is a separate executor per client, or a resilience library's bulkhead that caps concurrent calls and rejects the excess fast instead of queueing it. The key difference from a circuit breaker is timing: a bulkhead limits damage while calls are still being attempted, whereas a circuit breaker watches failures and stops calling a dependency entirely for a while. They are usually combined: the bulkhead bounds the blast radius and the breaker stops the bleeding. The trap is sizing: a pool that is too small rejects healthy traffic, and one that is too large is no bulkhead at all, so size each pool from the dependency's latency and the traffic you expect, and expose pool usage as a metric.
followUps: How do you size a bulkhead pool for a dependency?
Why combine a bulkhead with a circuit breaker instead of choosing one?
What happens when a bulkhead rejects a call?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the Bulkhead pattern, how do you implement it in a Spring Boot service, and how does it differ from a circuit breaker?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A bulkhead isolates resources per dependency, usually with separate thread pools or connection pools, so one slow dependency cannot consume everything; a circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency, while a bulkhead limits the damage while calls continue.
tips: Use the ship image, then the pool.
State the breaker difference as limit versus stop.
interviewQuestions.title: The Bulkhead pattern in practice

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: API evolution is a compatibility contract, not just a code change: adding a method to an interface breaks existing implementors, changing a return type or generic signature breaks callers, and renaming a public type breaks everyone, so stable APIs evolve by addition and deprecation, not by modification. A plugin or extension architecture should therefore depend on narrow, versioned interfaces, use composition over inheritance so hosts are not coupled to plugin internals, and isolate plugins with their own classloaders when versions of a shared library must coexist. Reflection and serialization bypass normal access rules and type checks, so they belong at system boundaries with explicit schemas and validation, not scattered through business logic. When a breaking change is unavoidable, ship it behind a new major version with a migration guide, dual support during transition, and telemetry showing the old API is actually unused before removal.
followUps: Why does adding a method to an interface break implementors?
When is a classloader boundary worth its complexity?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you design a public Java API and plugin system that can evolve without breaking its consumers?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Evolve by addition and deprecation, depend on narrow versioned interfaces, isolate plugins by classloader when needed, and remove old APIs only after telemetry proves they are unused.
tips: Frame compatibility as a contract, not a preference.
Name the interface-addition breakage — it is the classic trap.
interviewQuestions.title: API evolution and plugin design

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: At moderate scale the right collection is usually obvious, but at large scale the choice is driven by access pattern, memory overhead, and allocation behaviour, not by asymptotic complexity alone. An ArrayList of boxed objects costs far more memory and GC pressure than a primitive array or a specialized collection, a HashMap with a poor hash function degrades under adversarial keys, and a concurrent structure with high contention can be slower than a sharded or thread-local design. For ordered data, a balanced tree gives logarithmic ordered operations that a hash map cannot, and for streaming aggregation, a purpose-built accumulator avoids building intermediate collections entirely. The senior answer quantifies: estimate element count, per-element overhead, read-to-write ratio, and contention, then measure with a realistic workload, because a choice that is correct at ten thousand elements can be wrong at ten million.
followUps: When does a HashMap lose to a tree or a sorted array?
How do boxed primitives change the memory math?
interviewQuestions.question: How does collection choice change when a data structure must hold tens of millions of entries?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Beyond asymptotic complexity, decide on memory overhead, allocation and GC pressure, hash quality, ordering needs, and contention, and measure at realistic scale.
tips: Quantify: element count, overhead, read-write ratio, contention.
Name boxing overhead as the hidden cost most candidates miss.
interviewQuestions.title: Collections at scale

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Streams excel at declarative, in-memory transformation of finite data, but they are a poor fit for infinite or backpressured sources, for operations that need early exit with complex state, and for pipelines where checked exceptions or resource cleanup must be precise. A reactive stream, by contrast, models asynchronous data flow with demand signalling, so a slow consumer can slow the producer instead of being overwhelmed by an unbounded buffer. Mixing the two naively — collecting a reactive source into a list just to stream it, or blocking inside a reactive pipeline — loses the benefits of both. Choose plain streams for bounded in-memory work, reactive streams for asynchronous event flows with backpressure, and plain loops when the logic is stateful, exception-heavy, or performance-critical enough that stream overhead and boxing matter.
followUps: What does backpressure protect against that a plain stream cannot?
When is a plain loop better than a stream?
interviewQuestions.question: When should you not use Java Streams, and how does reactive streaming differ?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Streams suit bounded in-memory transformation; reactive streams add demand signalling for async flows, and plain loops win for stateful, exception-heavy, or allocation-sensitive code.
tips: Define backpressure in one sentence before comparing.
Give a concrete anti-pattern: collecting a reactive source just to re-stream it.
interviewQuestions.title: Streams versus reactive streams

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Lock-free algorithms use atomic compare-and-swap loops instead of locks, so a thread that fails a CAS retries rather than blocking, which avoids deadlock and keeps progress even when some threads stall, but retries under contention can burn CPU and the ABA problem can make a changed-then-restored value look unchanged. False sharing is the subtler trap: two threads updating different variables that share a cache line force the line to bounce between cores, so padding or grouping hot fields apart can yield large speedups in counters and queues. Distributed locking adds another layer: a lock held in Redis or a database must have a lease with expiry, a fencing token to reject stale holders after a pause, and a design that tolerates the lock holder dying, because a lock without expiry becomes a permanent outage. Prefer lock-free structures for single-JVM hot paths, and treat distributed locks as a coordination mechanism of last resort, with idempotent work underneath.
followUps: What is the ABA problem in a CAS loop?
Why does a distributed lock need a fencing token?
interviewQuestions.question: When do lock-free algorithms and distributed locks help, and what are their traps?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Lock-free CAS avoids blocking but risks retry storms and ABA; false sharing punishes nearby hot fields; distributed locks need leases and fencing tokens and should sit above idempotent work.
tips: Pair each technique with its specific trap.
Mention fencing tokens — they separate experienced answers from textbook ones.
interviewQuestions.title: Lock-free and distributed locking

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Low-latency collectors such as ZGC and Shenandoah keep pauses in the low milliseconds by doing most work concurrently with the application, at the cost of higher CPU overhead and throughput loss compared with G1 or Parallel. Tuning starts from a latency budget and a measurement: GC logs showing pause distribution, allocation rate, and heap occupancy, plus application latency percentiles, because average pause alone hides the tail that users feel. Escape analysis and JIT inlining reduce allocation in hot code, but they cannot rescue a design that allocates heavily per request, so the first optimization is usually fewer allocations, not more flags. For very large heaps or strict latency targets, evaluate the concurrent collector under production-like load and accept its CPU cost deliberately; for batch or throughput workloads, that trade is usually wrong.
followUps: Why is average GC pause a misleading metric?
When is a low-latency collector the wrong choice?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you choose and tune a garbage collector for a strict latency target?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Start from a latency budget and percentile measurements; ZGC and Shenandoah buy millisecond pauses with CPU overhead, so use them for latency-sensitive services and reduce allocation before tuning flags.
tips: Insist on percentiles, not averages.
State the throughput cost explicitly — it is a trade, not a free win.
interviewQuestions.title: Low-latency GC tuning

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Circular dependencies are usually a design smell: two beans needing each other at construction time means their responsibilities are tangled, and the honest fix is to extract the shared logic into a third bean or to invert the dependency. Spring can paper over some cycles with setter injection or proxies, but constructor injection rightly fails fast on a cycle, and suppressing that failure hides the design problem while making startup order fragile. Startup time in a large context comes from eager singleton creation, classpath scanning, and auto-configuration evaluation, so the remedies are lazy initialization for genuinely optional beans, narrower component scans, and fewer, more deliberate auto-configurations, measured with startup reports rather than guessed. For a modular monolith, enforce module boundaries with package rules and internal-only APIs, so the monolith stays decomposable instead of becoming a distributed monolith in disguise.
followUps: Why does constructor injection fail fast on a cycle while setter injection does not?
How do you keep a modular monolith decomposable?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you handle circular dependencies and slow startup in a large Spring application?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Treat cycles as a design smell to refactor, not to suppress; constructor injection failing fast is a feature, and startup improves with lazy beans, narrow scans, and measured auto-configuration costs.
tips: Take a position: refactor the cycle, do not work around it.
Mention package-boundary rules for modular monoliths.
interviewQuestions.title: Circular dependencies and startup time

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A custom starter should be a thin, opinionated packaging of auto-configuration, default properties, and dependencies, with every bean conditional so applications can override it, and with its own configuration properties namespace so settings do not collide. Multi-tenancy belongs in explicit layers: tenant resolution from a header or token, tenant-scoped data source routing or schema selection, and tenant context propagation through async boundaries, with tests that run the same scenario under two tenants. Observability is part of the starter contract: structured logs with correlation ids, metrics for the operations the starter performs, and health indicators that fail meaningfully rather than always reporting up. Graceful shutdown matters equally: stop accepting new work, drain in-flight requests within a timeout, and only then close resources, so rolling deploys do not drop requests.
followUps: How do you propagate tenant context across async boundaries?
What makes a health indicator meaningful rather than decorative?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you build a reusable Spring Boot starter for a multi-tenant platform?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Keep starters thin and conditional with their own properties namespace, resolve tenant explicitly and propagate it through async work, and include observability and graceful shutdown as part of the contract.
tips: List the starter contract: conditional beans, namespace, observability, shutdown.
Name tenant propagation across async boundaries as the hard part.
interviewQuestions.title: Custom starters and multi-tenancy

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: API versioning is a compatibility strategy, not a URL prefix: version in the URI for coarse, client-visible breaking changes, in headers or content negotiation when clients can handle it, and prefer backwards-compatible evolution — additive fields, optional parameters, and tolerant readers — so most changes need no version at all. Contract tests, where consumers publish the expectations they rely on, catch breaking changes before release far more reliably than manual coordination, and a deprecation policy with sunset headers and usage telemetry tells you when an old version can actually be retired. Rate limiting and request validation belong at the gateway or filter layer for coarse protection, with fine-grained business limits in the service layer where domain context lives. Never version by forking controller code without a shared core, or the versions will drift and a bug fix will land in one version only.
followUps: When can you avoid versioning entirely?
How do you know when an old API version is safe to retire?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you version a public API and retire old versions without breaking clients?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Prefer backwards-compatible evolution, version coarsely when breaking, enforce compatibility with consumer contract tests, and retire versions only on telemetry plus a published sunset policy.
tips: Lead with backwards-compatible evolution, not versioning schemes.
Name consumer contract tests as the enforcement mechanism.
interviewQuestions.title: API versioning and contract tests

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: JPA excels at single-database domain modelling, but it strains at scale in three places: a single write database becomes a bottleneck, a shared entity graph couples read and write shapes, and lazy loading plus the persistence context add overhead to bulk work. The standard responses are read replicas for read-heavy workloads with explicit tolerance for replication lag, CQRS read models that precompute the shapes queries actually need, and bulk operations through JDBC or batch statements that bypass the persistence context for imports and updates. Sharding is a last resort, not a first step, because it breaks joins, transactions, and reporting across shards and forces application-level routing and rebalancing. The senior judgement is knowing which scale problem you actually have — read volume, write volume, or data volume — because each has a different remedy.
followUps: When does a read replica hurt rather than help?
Why is sharding a last resort?
interviewQuestions.question: Where does JPA break down at scale, and what replaces each piece?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use read replicas for read volume, CQRS read models for mismatched read shapes, and JDBC batching for bulk work; reserve sharding for data volume it alone can solve, since it breaks joins and transactions.
tips: Diagnose the scale problem first: reads, writes, or data volume.
Warn that replication lag makes replicas unsuitable for read-after-write flows.
interviewQuestions.title: JPA at scale: replicas, CQRS, sharding

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Event-driven architecture decouples producers from consumers in time and in topology, but it trades immediate consistency for eventual consistency, and that trade must be visible in the product: user interfaces need pending states, and business processes need compensations for late or failed events. Schema evolution is the long-term cost, so events should be versioned, backwards-compatible, and self-describing, with consumers tolerating unknown fields and producers never reusing a field name for a new meaning. Every consumer must be idempotent with a stored record of processed event ids, because at-least-once delivery guarantees duplicates, and every event flow needs dead-letter handling, replay capability, and distributed tracing across producer and consumer. If a workflow needs an immediate, synchronous answer, an event is the wrong tool — use a request-response call and reserve events for facts other services react to.
followUps: How do you make an event consumer safe to replay?
When is an event the wrong choice versus a synchronous call?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you design an event-driven system that survives duplicates, schema changes, and failures?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Design for eventual consistency with pending states and compensations, version events compatibly, make consumers idempotent, and provide dead-letter handling, replay, and end-to-end tracing.
tips: Name the product consequence of eventual consistency, not just the pattern.
Insist on stored processed-event ids for idempotency.
interviewQuestions.title: Event-driven architecture at scale

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: At very large tables, query design is index design: range queries need the range column last in a composite index after equality columns, selective filters beat broad ones, and sorting without an index forces a costly sort of the full result. Partitioning by a natural key such as time lets old partitions be archived or dropped cheaply and keeps working sets small, but queries that do not filter on the partition key must scan every partition. Locking behaviour matters as much as speed: long transactions hold locks and block writers, gap locks under repeatable read can deadlock concurrent inserts, and the remedy is usually shorter transactions, consistent lock ordering, and retrying deadlocked transactions rather than raising timeouts. Always verify with the execution plan on production-sized data, because a plan that is fine at a million rows can be catastrophic at a hundred million.
followUps: Why should the range column come last in a composite index?
How do you reduce deadlocks without raising timeouts?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you design indexes, partitioning, and transactions for tables with hundreds of millions of rows?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Order composite indexes equality-first and range-last, partition on the key queries actually filter by, keep transactions short with consistent lock ordering, and verify plans at production scale.
tips: Give the composite-index ordering rule concretely.
Name gap locks as the deadlock mechanism, not just deadlocks in general.
interviewQuestions.title: SQL at very large scale

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The task is to design a rate limiter that works across multiple service instances. The idiomatic approach is a token-bucket or fixed-window counter per key, stored in a shared store with an atomic increment and expiry, so every instance observes the same count. A single-instance in-memory limiter is correct only until the second instance deploys, at which point each instance enforces its own limit and the effective limit multiplies. For strict fairness, use a shared atomic counter with a window, accept the small race window of fixed windows or the complexity of a sliding-window log, and return a standard too-many-requests response with a retry-after hint. Edge cases to name are clock skew between instances, hot keys that concentrate on one store shard, and the failure mode when the store itself is unavailable — fail open for non-critical endpoints, fail closed for abuse-sensitive ones.
followUps: Why does a per-instance limiter break when you scale out?
Should the limiter fail open or fail closed when its store is down?
interviewQuestions.question: Coding task: design a rate limiter that stays correct when the service scales to many instances. What is your approach?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use a shared atomic counter per key with a window in a central store, such as a token bucket, so all instances share one limit; per-instance counters multiply the limit on scale-out.
tips: Start from the scale-out failure of in-memory limiters.
Name the fail-open versus fail-closed decision for store outages.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: distributed rate limiter

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Apply the strangler pattern: put the new service behind the existing monolith's interface, route a slice of traffic or a single capability to it, and expand slice by slice, so every step is reversible and the old system remains the fallback. Data is the hard part: keep a single source of truth during transition, synchronize with change-data-capture or dual writes guarded by reconciliation jobs, and migrate data in small, verifiable batches with checksums rather than one big cutover. Rollback means routing traffic back and reconciling any writes the new service made, which only works if writes are idempotent and the old system can still accept them, so design the new service's writes with that constraint from day one. Success criteria are not the migration itself but the metrics that prove it: error rates, latency, and data-consistency checks at each slice, with a named owner and a decision point for each expansion.
followUps: Why is a big-bang cutover riskier than strangler migration?
How do you reconcile data written by the new service during rollback?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: you must extract a payment capability from a monolith into a service without downtime. How do you plan it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Strangle it slice by slice behind the old interface, keep one source of truth with reconciled synchronization, migrate data in verifiable batches, and make rollback possible via idempotent writes.
tips: Lead with the strangler pattern and reversibility.
Name data reconciliation, not just traffic routing, as the hard part.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: strangler migration

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: First, establish scope and reversibility: confirm the regression with a controlled comparison, such as canary traffic on the old and new versions under the same load, and check whether the change is the JDK, a library upgrade shipped with it, or a configuration change that rode along. Then narrow with evidence in order: GC logs and pause percentiles, JIT compilation and deoptimization logs, thread and CPU profiles, and dependency changelogs, looking for a behaviour change in a collector, a hashing order, or a default that the application silently depended on. As a staff-level decision, you would halt the rollout at the canary stage, keep the old version deployable, and choose between pinning the old version, tuning the new one, or fixing the application assumption, based on which evidence you have and how long each path takes. The post-incident action is a regression gate: a performance benchmark and a canary comparison in the upgrade pipeline, so the next JDK upgrade cannot regress silently.
followUps: How do you separate a JDK regression from a library or config change shipped with it?
When do you roll back versus tune forward?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: after a JDK upgrade, latency percentiles regress in production. As the technical lead, how do you investigate and decide?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Compare canary versions under identical load, narrow with GC, JIT, and profile evidence, halt the rollout, and decide between rollback, tuning, or fixing the app assumption based on evidence and time to fix.
tips: Lead with the canary comparison, not with a guess about the collector.
Frame the decision explicitly: rollback, tune, or fix — with criteria.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: JDK upgrade regression
Coding: duplicate elements and their counts with streams
interviewQuestions.question: Coding task: given a list of integers, find the elements that appear more than once, together with how many times each appears, using the Stream API.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Group the list by element with a count, then keep only the entries whose count is greater than one.
followUps: What is the time and memory cost of this approach?
How would you return the duplicates sorted by how often they appear?
tips: Name the two-step shape: group and count, then filter.
Walk through a small example so the interviewer sees the map taking shape.
commonMistakes: Sorting the list first and comparing neighbours, which is slower and more code.
Using a Set to detect duplicates but losing the counts the question asked for.

interviewQuestions.title: Coding: highest-paid employee per department with streams
interviewQuestions.question: Coding task: given a list of employees with a name, a department, and a salary, find the highest-paid employee in each department using the Stream API.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Group by department, and inside each group reduce with maxBy on salary.
followUps: How would you unwrap the Optional in the result, and when is that safe?
What happens if two employees in one department share the top salary?
tips: Say the pattern name: a downstream collector inside groupingBy.
Name the tie behaviour before the interviewer asks.
commonMistakes: Sorting the whole list and taking the first per department, which is wasteful and fiddly.
Forgetting that maxBy returns an Optional and trying to use the result as a plain employee.

interviewQuestions.title: CountDownLatch versus CyclicBarrier
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between CountDownLatch and CyclicBarrier, and when would you pick each one?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A latch is a one-shot gate that waits for a set of events; a barrier is a reusable meeting point where a set of threads wait for each other.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
A CountDownLatch is created with a count, other threads call countDown() as work finishes, and one or more waiting threads are released when the count reaches zero. It cannot be reset, so it fits one-off waits: a main thread waiting for several workers to finish initialising, or a test waiting for asynchronous callbacks. The waiting thread does not have to be one of the counting threads.

A CyclicBarrier is created with a number of parties, and every party must call await() before any of them is released, so the threads wait for each other rather than for outside events. It resets itself after each trip, so it fits repeated rounds of work, such as parallel computation that synchronises at the end of each step, and it can run a barrier action once per round when all parties arrive. A broken barrier, for example when a thread times out or is interrupted while waiting, trips the barrier for everyone, which is a failure mode a latch does not have.

The interview-ready rule: use a latch when one thread waits for many events to happen, and a barrier when many threads must arrive together before any of them continues.
followUps: What happens to a CyclicBarrier if one waiting thread is interrupted?
How would you wait for several services to finish starting up before taking traffic?
tips: Lead with the one-line contrast: one-shot gate versus reusable meeting point.
Give one concrete use for each instead of only describing the API.
commonMistakes: Saying the two are interchangeable because both make threads wait.
Forgetting that a latch cannot be reused and a barrier releases only when every party arrives.

interviewQuestions.title: ThreadPoolExecutor internals: sizing, queues, and rejection
interviewQuestions.question: Explain how ThreadPoolExecutor actually works inside: core threads, maximum threads, the work queue, and what happens when the pool is saturated.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: New tasks go to a core thread first, then to the queue, then to extra threads up to the maximum, and finally to the rejection policy; the queue type decides most of the behaviour.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
The order of decisions is the part most candidates get wrong. When a task arrives, the pool starts a new core thread if fewer than corePoolSize threads are running. Otherwise the task goes onto the work queue. Only when the queue is full does the pool grow beyond the core size, up to maximumPoolSize. If the pool is at its maximum and the queue is full, the rejection policy runs.

That makes the queue the most important sizing choice. An unbounded queue, which is what the Executors.newFixedThreadPool shortcut uses, means the pool never grows past its core size and can instead grow memory without bound under load, which is how services run out of memory during a slow downstream outage. A bounded queue with a sensible limit plus a rejection policy such as CallerRunsPolicy, which pushes back on the caller, or AbortPolicy with a clear error, gives you a visible, controllable failure instead.

Also name the supporting details: keep-alive time applies to threads above the core size, worker threads pull tasks from the queue in a loop, and a rejected task after shutdown is a separate case from a saturated pool. The senior answer ends with a rule of thumb: size core threads to the work, CPU-bound near the core count and I/O-bound higher, bound the queue, and choose the rejection policy deliberately.
followUps: Why can an unbounded queue make a fixed thread pool run out of memory?
When would you pick CallerRunsPolicy over AbortPolicy?
tips: State the order: core thread, then queue, then extra threads, then rejection.
Name the unbounded-queue trap in the Executors factory shortcuts.
commonMistakes: Saying the pool grows to its maximum before using the queue.
Treating the queue size as unimportant when it actually controls saturation behaviour.

interviewQuestions.title: Strong, soft, weak, and phantom references, and cache memory leaks
interviewQuestions.question: What are the four reference types in Java, and how do they explain the classic memory leak where a cache keeps growing forever?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Strong references pin objects in memory; soft references are cleared under memory pressure, weak ones at the next collection, and phantom ones only signal cleanup. A cache of strong references is a leak by design.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
A strong reference is an ordinary reference: as long as it is reachable, the garbage collector will not reclaim the object. A soft reference is cleared when the JVM is short of memory, which makes it the right tool for a memory-sensitive cache. A weak reference is cleared at the next collection once no strong reference remains, which is how WeakHashMap lets entries disappear when their keys are no longer used elsewhere. A phantom reference cannot even be used to reach the object; it exists so cleanup code can be notified through a ReferenceQueue after the object is collected, and it is the mechanism behind the cleaner API that replaced finalizers.

The classic cache leak is a static map, or a long-lived collection, holding strong references to objects that are never removed: entries accumulate, the heap grows, and eventually the application fails with an OutOfMemoryError even though nothing is logically still needed. Other versions of the same leak are listeners that are never unregistered, ThreadLocal values left behind on pooled threads, and classloaders pinned by a single stray reference after a redeploy.

The fix depends on the intent: bound the cache with a size or time limit and an eviction policy, use soft or weak references where the cache is genuinely allowed to lose entries, and always remove what you registered. When diagnosing, look at what dominates the heap in a heap dump and follow the reference chain back to the GC root that keeps it alive.
followUps: When would you choose a soft reference over a weak reference for a cache?
How does a ThreadLocal leak happen on a pooled thread?
tips: Order the four types by how eagerly the collector clears them.
Trace the leak to a GC root in the heap dump, not just to the growing collection.
commonMistakes: Saying weak references are cleared only under memory pressure; that is soft references.
Treating a cache as harmless because it is only a map, while it holds strong references forever.

interviewQuestions.title: Dynamic proxies in Java and how Spring uses them
interviewQuestions.question: What are dynamic proxies in Java, how do you create one, and where does Spring rely on them?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A dynamic proxy is a runtime-generated object that implements an interface and forwards every call to an InvocationHandler, which is how Spring adds behaviour such as transactions around a bean.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
A JDK dynamic proxy is created at runtime with Proxy.newProxyInstance, given a classloader, the interfaces to implement, and an InvocationHandler whose invoke method receives every method call. The handler can run code before and after the call, decide whether to call the real object at all, change arguments or results, and wrap exceptions. Because the proxy is built from interfaces, it can only stand in for an interface type, never for a concrete class.

Spring uses this mechanism in several places. Transactional methods, security checks, and asynchronous execution are applied by wrapping a bean in a proxy that adds the extra behaviour around the real method. When a bean implements an interface, Spring's default is a JDK dynamic proxy; when it does not, Spring falls back to a subclass-based proxy, historically CGLIB. That split explains two famous gotchas: a call from one method of a bean to another method of the same bean bypasses the proxy entirely, so a transactional annotation on the inner method is silently ignored, and final methods cannot be intercepted by a subclass proxy.

Good interview answers name a legitimate use of proxies beyond Spring: a logging or metrics wrapper, a lazy-loading stand-in, or a remote stub. They also name the cost: an extra indirection per call, stack traces that are harder to read, and behaviour that is invisible in the source code of the class itself.
followUps: Why does a self-call inside a bean skip transaction handling?
When does Spring switch from a JDK proxy to a subclass proxy?
tips: Start from the three inputs to newProxyInstance: classloader, interfaces, handler.
Connect the interface-only limit directly to the Spring self-invocation trap.
commonMistakes: Saying a dynamic proxy can wrap any class; it can only implement interfaces.
Forgetting that behaviour added by a proxy is invisible when reading the target class.

interviewQuestions.title: The Java module system (JPMS) for a modular monolith
interviewQuestions.question: How would you use the Java 9 module system to turn a monolith into a genuinely modular application, and what are the practical costs?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Give each part a module-info file that declares what it needs and what it exports, so package boundaries become compiler-enforced instead of conventions.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
A module is a named group of packages with a module-info.java file. It declares requires for the modules it depends on and exports only the packages other modules may use; everything else is encapsulated, even public classes in non-exported packages. The opens directive exists for the frameworks that need deep reflection, such as serialization libraries and dependency injection containers, which is a deliberate hole you should keep as narrow as possible.

For a monolith, the practical path is to draw the boundaries first, usually one module per bounded context or layer, and then migrate bottom-up, starting with the libraries with the fewest dependencies, or top-down, starting with the application modules. Old jars without a module descriptor land on the classpath as the unnamed module or on the module path as automatic modules, which lets migration happen in stages, but split packages, where the same package exists in two jars, and reflective access from old frameworks are the two problems that actually block teams.

Be honest about the payoff at senior level: JPMS gives you strong encapsulation, a smaller runtime image with jlink, and reliable configuration that fails fast on a missing module, but it does not by itself give you a microservices architecture, and many teams decide the build and reflection friction is not worth it for an application that already enforces boundaries with build modules and package rules.
followUps: What is a split package, and why does JPMS refuse it?
When would you choose build modules over JPMS modules?
tips: Frame modules as compiler-enforced boundaries, not just packaging.
Name automatic modules as the realistic migration bridge.
commonMistakes: Claiming JPMS alone makes a system a microservices architecture.
Opening every package to reflection and defeating the encapsulation JPMS was added for.

interviewQuestions.title: Metaspace, PermGen, and diagnosing OutOfMemoryError
interviewQuestions.question: What is Metaspace, how does it differ from PermGen, and how would you investigate an OutOfMemoryError in production?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Metaspace replaced PermGen in Java 8 and holds class metadata in native memory with no fixed default limit; an OutOfMemoryError there usually means classes or classloaders are leaking.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Before Java 8, class metadata lived in PermGen, a fixed-size area inside the Java heap that filled up with too many classes and had to be tuned with PermSize and MaxPermSize. Since Java 8, the same metadata lives in Metaspace, which is allocated from native memory and by default grows until the operating system runs out of memory, with MaxMetaspaceSize as an optional cap. That removes the old tuning chore but changes the failure: Metaspace growth no longer throws a heap error, it consumes native memory, and the usual cause is a classloader leak, where a classloader and all its classes are pinned by a stray reference after a redeploy, or an application that generates classes without bound, such as dynamic proxies or runtime bytecode.

Investigating an OutOfMemoryError starts with which error it is, because the fix is different each time: Java heap space means live objects or a leak in the heap, GC overhead limit exceeded means the collector is spending nearly all its time collecting almost nothing, and Metaspace means classes or classloaders. Enable heap dumps on OutOfMemoryError so the evidence survives the crash, look at what dominates the heap or Metaspace in the dump, and check GC logs for the allocation and pause trend before the failure. A classloader leak shows up as many duplicate classloaders holding the same classes, and the fix is to find and break the reference that pins the old loader, not to raise a limit.
followUps: Why can raising MaxMetaspaceSize make a classloader leak worse instead of fixing it?
How do you tell a genuine heap shortage apart from a leak?
tips: Start by naming which OutOfMemoryError it is; the fixes are different.
Name the classloader leak as the classic Metaspace cause after redeploys.
commonMistakes: Raising the heap or Metaspace limit without finding what is growing.
Treating every OutOfMemoryError as a heap problem.

interviewQuestions.title: Spring AOP: join points, pointcuts, and where it breaks down
interviewQuestions.question: Explain Spring AOP in plain terms: join points, pointcuts, and advice, and when is AOP the wrong tool?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: AOP adds behaviour around method executions matched by a pointcut; it is proxy-based, so it only sees calls that pass through a Spring bean proxy.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
A join point is a point in the program where extra behaviour can be attached; in Spring AOP that is always a method execution. A pointcut is the expression that selects which methods match, for example all public methods in a service package. Advice is the extra behaviour itself, run before, after, or around the matched method, and an aspect is the class that bundles pointcuts and advice together.

Spring AOP works through proxies, which sets its limits. It can only intercept method calls on Spring beans that go through the proxy, so a call from one method to another method of the same bean bypasses the advice entirely, and it cannot intercept field access, constructors, or calls on objects Spring does not manage. Full AspectJ with compile-time or load-time weaving removes those limits but adds build complexity.

AOP earns its place for cross-cutting concerns that would otherwise be pasted into every method: logging, metrics, security checks, and transactions. It is the wrong tool when the behaviour is core business logic that belongs in the method itself, when the flow becomes hard to follow because behaviour is invisible at the call site, or when a simple decorator or an explicit call would say the same thing more clearly. The senior answer names the debugging cost directly: with AOP, reading a method no longer tells you everything that happens when it runs.
followUps: Why does a self-call inside a bean skip an aspect?
When would you reach for full AspectJ instead of Spring AOP?
tips: Define the three terms in one sentence each, then move to the limits.
Name the invisible-behaviour cost; it is the senior judgement.
commonMistakes: Saying AOP can intercept any code, including field access and constructors, in Spring.
Putting business logic in an aspect where nobody will look for it.

interviewQuestions.title: Caching done right: stale data, eviction, and stampedes
interviewQuestions.question: How do you use caching in a Spring Boot application without serving stale data or collapsing under a cache stampede?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Cache with a short TTL and explicit eviction on writes, and make sure a cache miss is cheap or single-flighted so a cold cache cannot hammer the database.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Spring's cache abstraction, @Cacheable to fill, @CacheEvict to clear, and @CachePut to refresh, is only the entry point; the real design is about invalidation. Every write path that changes the underlying data must evict or update the affected entries, or the cache will serve stale data until the time-to-live expires. A short TTL bounds how wrong the data can be, and versioning the cache key or the payload lets clients detect a stale read. Choosing a cache-aside pattern, where the application reads through the cache and fills it on a miss, keeps the database as the source of truth.

The second failure is the stampede: when a popular entry expires, many concurrent requests all miss at once and hit the database together. Mitigations are to refresh entries before they expire, to let one request refill while others wait briefly, or to stagger expiry times so entries do not all expire together. A local cache such as Caffeine is fast but is per-instance, so an eviction on one instance does not clear the others; a shared cache such as Redis is consistent across instances but adds a network hop and a new failure mode. The senior answer always names what happens when the cache is down: the application must fall back to the database, slowly, rather than failing every request.
followUps: Why is a local cache dangerous for eviction in a multi-instance service?
What should the application do when the cache itself is unavailable?
tips: Talk about invalidation before you talk about filling the cache.
Name the stampede as the failure that only appears at real traffic.
commonMistakes: Caching without an eviction path on writes and relying on TTL alone.
Treating a cache miss storm as a database problem instead of a caching design problem.

interviewQuestions.title: Zero-downtime deployment and safe rollback for Spring Boot
interviewQuestions.question: How do you deploy a new version of a Spring Boot service with zero downtime, and how do you roll back safely when the new version is bad?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Roll out instance by instance behind readiness checks with graceful shutdown, keep database changes backwards compatible, and make rollback a redeploy of the known-good version.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Zero downtime is a sequence, not a single feature.
