The new version starts, waits until it is genuinely ready, and only then receives traffic, which is what the readiness probe is for; a service that reports ready before its connections and caches are warm will fail its first real requests. The old instance stops accepting new work, finishes the requests it already has within a timeout, and only then shuts down, which is graceful shutdown, enabled with server.shutdown=graceful in Spring Boot. A rolling deploy repeats this one instance at a time, while blue-green and canary deploys add the ability to shift a slice of traffic and watch it before committing.

The part teams most often get wrong is the database. A new version must work with the old schema and the old version must work with the new schema during the transition, which is the expand-and-contract pattern: add a column first, deploy code that writes both shapes, then remove the old shape in a later release. A migration that renames or drops a column in the same deploy as the code that needs it is a guaranteed outage.

Rollback must be boring: redeploy the previous artifact, which only works if artifacts are versioned and the database change was backwards compatible. The decision to roll back should be made on metrics, error rate and latency at the canary stage, not on a feeling, and the runbook should say in advance who decides and how long the canary runs.
followUps: Why does a column rename break a rolling deploy?
What does the readiness probe check that the liveness probe does not?
tips: Walk the deploy as a sequence: ready, shift traffic, drain, stop.
Name expand-and-contract as the database rule.
commonMistakes: Reporting ready before the application can actually serve traffic.
Shipping a breaking database migration in the same release as the code that depends on it.

interviewQuestions.title: Distributed tracing: trace IDs, spans, and Micrometer Tracing
interviewQuestions.question: How does distributed tracing work in a Spring Boot microservice system, and what changed when Sleuth was replaced by Micrometer Tracing?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Each request gets a trace ID shared by all services it touches, with a span per operation; Micrometer Tracing is the Boot 3 replacement for Sleuth that bridges to OpenTelemetry or Brave.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
A trace is the whole journey of one request across services, identified by a trace ID that is passed along in headers, and a span is one step in that journey, such as a controller call or a downstream request, identified by a span ID with a parent span ID linking it to the step that called it. With those three identifiers, logs and traces from many services can be joined into one timeline, which is what makes a slow request debuggable: you can see which service and which call actually consumed the time, instead of guessing from separate log files.

In Spring Boot 3, Sleuth was replaced by Micrometer Tracing. The concepts are the same, but the setup is different: you add Micrometer Tracing with a bridge to your tracing backend, OpenTelemetry or Brave, and a span exporter or collector such as Zipkin or an OpenTelemetry collector, and the trace and span IDs are put into the logging context automatically so every log line carries them. Sampling decides how many traces are recorded; keeping every trace is too expensive at scale, so production systems usually sample a fraction of normal traces and keep all error traces.

The practical pitfalls are propagation and context loss: the trace ID must travel across every hop, including message queues and asynchronous work, or the trace breaks into pieces, and a thread pool that does not copy the context will log work under the wrong trace. The senior answer names both and says how to check: follow one request end to end in the trace view and confirm no hop is missing.
followUps: Why do logs need the trace ID in them, not just the tracing UI?
What breaks tracing when work moves to another thread or a queue?
tips: Define trace, span, and the three IDs before describing any library.
Name sampling as the cost control, not an afterthought.
commonMistakes: Assuming tracing works automatically across async boundaries and message queues.
Keeping every trace in production and paying for it in storage and overhead.

interviewQuestions.title: WebFlux versus Spring MVC: when reactive is worth it
interviewQuestions.question: When should you choose Spring WebFlux over Spring MVC, and what is the mistake that ruins most first WebFlux projects?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Choose WebFlux when many concurrent, mostly idle connections must share few threads; the classic mistake is blocking inside a reactive pipeline.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Spring MVC gives each request a thread from a pool and blocks it while waiting for a database or a downstream call, which is simple and works well until the thread pool itself becomes the bottleneck. WebFlux runs on a small number of event-loop threads and never blocks them: work is expressed as publishers, Mono for zero or one result and Flux for many, and a thread picks up the next piece of work while an earlier one waits for I/O. That pays off for workloads with very high concurrency and lots of waiting, such as gateways, proxies, and streaming endpoints, where thousands of connections are open but mostly idle.

The mistake that ruins first WebFlux projects is blocking inside the pipeline: calling a blocking database driver, doing a slow computation, or taking a lock on an event-loop thread stalls every request sharing that thread. Blocking work must move to a dedicated scheduler for blocking calls or be replaced with a non-blocking client, such as a reactive database driver. Other honest costs are a harder debugging experience, with stack traces that cross asynchronous boundaries, and a smaller ecosystem of blocking libraries that need wrapping.

The senior rule is to choose on the workload, not on fashion: a typical CRUD service backed by a blocking database gains nothing from WebFlux and pays for complexity it does not need, while a gateway or a fan-out service with long-lived connections is where reactive earns its keep.
followUps: What happens if you call a blocking JDBC query inside a WebFlux handler?
How does backpressure protect a fast producer from a slow consumer?
tips: Lead with the workload shape, not the framework names.
Name the blocking-call mistake explicitly; interviewers wait for it.
commonMistakes: Adopting WebFlux for a standard CRUD service and gaining only complexity.
Blocking an event-loop thread and stalling unrelated requests.

interviewQuestions.title: Securing a REST API with JWT and OAuth2
interviewQuestions.question: How would you secure a REST API in Spring Boot end to end, using JWT and OAuth2, and what are the traps?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Put TLS in front, authenticate with OAuth2 and short-lived signed JWTs, authorise by roles or scopes, and validate every token's signature, expiry, audience, and issuer.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Start outside the code: the API is only reachable over TLS, tokens are never sent over plain HTTP, and the service sits behind rate limiting so a stolen token cannot be replayed at full speed. Authentication uses OAuth2: the client obtains a token from an authorization server, for example with the authorization code flow for users or the client credentials flow for services, and sends it as a bearer token. The resource server validates the token on every request: the signature against the authorization server's keys, the expiry, and the audience and issuer claims, so a token minted for another API or another environment is rejected.

A JWT is a signed container, not a vault: its header, payload, and signature are base64-encoded and readable by anyone, so it must never carry secrets or personal data, and its claims should be the minimum the API needs, such as the user id, roles, and scopes. Tokens are short-lived, with refresh tokens used to get new ones, and logout means the token simply expires, unless you keep a denylist, which is a trade-off most stateless designs accept. In Spring Boot this is configured as a resource server with a JWT decoder and method or URL rules that map scopes and roles to endpoints.

The traps to name: trusting a token without validating its signature, accepting tokens with no expiry, putting sensitive data in claims, and storing tokens in a place JavaScript can read when a cookie with the HttpOnly flag would have been safer.
followUps: How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?
Why must a JWT never contain secrets even though it is signed?
tips: Walk the request: TLS, token, validation, authorisation, in that order.
Say what a JWT is not: it is not encryption.
commonMistakes: Validating only that a token exists, not its signature, expiry, audience, and issuer.
Putting sensitive data into JWT claims because they look protected.

interviewQuestions.title: Service-to-service security in microservices
interviewQuestions.question: How do services authenticate and authorise each other in a microservices system, and why is a user token not enough?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Give each service its own identity with short-lived credentials and mutual TLS, and check authorisation at every service, not just at the edge.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
A user token proves who the user is, but it says nothing about which service is calling, and once it is inside the network it can be passed along by any service, including one that was compromised. Each service therefore needs its own identity: mutual TLS, where both sides present certificates and verify each other, is the strongest common answer, and short-lived service tokens from the client credentials flow are the lighter alternative. Secrets and certificates come from a vault or a certificate manager with rotation, never from a config file checked into source control.

Authorisation must also be checked at every service, not only at the gateway: a service that trusts any internal caller is one breach away from full access, so each service verifies the caller's identity and whether that identity may perform the operation. The user token still travels with the request for user-level authorisation, but it is validated again at each hop rather than trusted because it arrived on an internal network.

The honest trade-offs are operational: certificate rotation, clock skew between services, and debugging a request that fails authentication in the middle of a chain. The senior answer names a concrete check for the design: revoke one service's credentials and confirm that exactly that service loses access while everything else keeps working.
followUps: Why is trusting the internal network alone not a security model?
How would you test that revoking one service's credentials works?
tips: Separate the two identities: the user and the calling service.
Name the revocation test as proof the design works.
commonMistakes: Passing the user token along and treating any internal call as trusted.
Hard-coding service secrets in configuration files.

interviewQuestions.title: Database per service: the trade-offs and the consistency bill
interviewQuestions.question: Why does each microservice get its own database, and what do you lose when you can no longer join across services?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A private database keeps services independently deployable and scalable, but cross-service joins and transactions become API calls, events, or sagas.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
A private database per service is what makes services genuinely independent: one team can change its schema, scale its storage, or even pick a different database technology without coordinating a shared schema change with every other team, and a failure or a heavy query in one service cannot lock tables that another service needs. A shared database quietly re-couples services that look independent on a diagram, because every schema change becomes a negotiation.

The bill arrives in three places. First, reading data that lives in two services can no longer be a join; it becomes an API call, a replicated read model, or a query service that joins data it has copied. Second, a write that spans services can no longer be one transaction; it becomes a saga with compensating actions or an outbox that publishes an event after the local commit. Third, reporting across services needs its own pipeline, because there is no single database to query.

The judgement call is to choose the mechanism per use case: synchronous API calls when the caller needs an immediate answer, events and replicated read models when eventual consistency is acceptable, and a saga when a multi-step write must be undone cleanly. The interview answer that stands out names the consistency the business actually needs before picking a mechanism, because most cross-service reads tolerate a short delay, and the ones that do not should be designed as a single service boundary instead.
followUps: When would you accept a shared database despite the coupling?
How do you build a report that needs data from five services?
tips: Start with the independence the pattern buys, then present the bill.
Pick the mechanism from the consistency the business needs.
commonMistakes: Reaching for a distributed transaction as the first answer to cross-service writes.
Joining across services by giving one service direct access to another's tables.

interviewQuestions.title: The API Gateway pattern: what it owns and what breaks it
interviewQuestions.question: What does an API Gateway do in a microservices architecture, and what goes wrong when it owns too much?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The gateway is the single entry point that routes, authenticates, rate-limits, and aggregates; it breaks when business logic or service-specific rules creep into it.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Clients talk to one stable address, and the gateway routes each request to the right service, terminates TLS, checks authentication, enforces rate limits, and adds cross-cutting behaviour such as request logging, correlation IDs, and response caching. It can also aggregate several downstream calls into one response for a client, which is the backend-for-frontend variant, where each client type gets a gateway tailored to its needs.

The gateway earns its place by removing duplicated plumbing from every service, but it has two failure modes. The first is availability: it is a single entry point, so it must itself be deployed redundantly and must fail gracefully, shedding load rather than taking the whole system down. The second is scope creep: when business logic, service-specific validation, or data transformation moves into the gateway, it becomes a distributed monolith that every team must change and that no team owns. Routing, security, and traffic policy belong in the gateway; domain rules belong in the services.

A good answer also names the alternative: direct client-to-service calls with service discovery, which removes the hop and the bottleneck but pushes routing, authentication, and versioning onto every client. The choice is a trade-off between a central choke point with consistent policy and a decentralised design with duplicated client logic.
followUps: When would you use a backend-for-frontend instead of one shared gateway?
How do you keep the gateway itself highly available?
tips: List what the gateway owns, then draw the line where its ownership stops.
Name the alternative so the trade-off is visible.
commonMistakes: Putting domain logic in the gateway until it becomes a monolith in disguise.
Treating the gateway as free and forgetting it adds latency and a failure point.

interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: rescuing a project that is slipping badly
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: as the technical lead, you inherit a project that is weeks behind schedule with low morale and no clear picture of what is actually done. How do you recover it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: First get a truthful picture of what is done and what is blocking, then cut scope with stakeholders, stabilise the plan in short cycles, and protect the team from further churn.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
The first move is diagnosis, not heroics: build an honest inventory of what is genuinely finished, what is half done, and what is blocked, by looking at the work itself rather than status reports, and talk to the team privately to learn what is actually slowing them down. A project that is behind usually has a small number of real blockers, such as an unclear requirement, a flaky dependency, or one overloaded person, hiding behind a long list of tasks.

The second move is to re-plan with stakeholders, not for them: present the real state, offer explicit trade-offs between scope, date, and quality, and agree a smaller, credible scope with a short, visible cadence, such as weekly demonstrable progress, so trust is rebuilt with evidence rather than promises. Cutting scope is a decision stakeholders must own; silently dropping quality is not a recovery plan.

The third move is to protect the team's ability to deliver: remove or sequence the blockers, limit work in progress so half-finished work stops multiplying, and stop adding new scope until the plan is stable. Morale recovers when people see progress and when overtime is not the plan. The answer that stands out names the trap explicitly: adding more people to a late project usually slows it further while they learn the codebase, so the recovery is about focus and unblocking, not headcount.
followUps: How do you tell stakeholders the date will slip without losing their trust?
What do you do if the main blocker is a person the project depends on?
tips: Lead with diagnosis from the work itself, not from status reports.
Make scope cuts an explicit stakeholder decision, not a silent quality cut.
commonMistakes: Adding people to a late project as the first response.
Promising a new date before finding out what is actually unfinished.

interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: handling scope creep and aligning tech with business goals
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: stakeholders keep adding features mid-sprint while the deadline stays fixed. As a senior developer and tech lead, how do you handle it, and how do you keep technical work aligned with business goals?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Make every addition an explicit trade-off: estimate its cost, show what it displaces, and let stakeholders choose, tying each item to the business outcome it serves.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Scope creep is rarely malice; it is usually a request that sounds small and whose cost is invisible. The response is to make the cost visible: estimate the new work honestly, show what would have to be dropped or delayed to fit it in, and put the choice back to the stakeholders instead of absorbing it silently. A simple rule helps: new work enters through the same prioritisation as existing work, and nothing jumps the queue without displacing something.

Alignment with business goals works the same way, by translation. A technical item earns its place by the business outcome it serves: a refactoring that unblocks a revenue feature, a performance fix that reduces churn, or a reliability investment that protects a launch. When you present technical work in those terms, stakeholders can weigh it against features fairly, and you stop being the person who says no and become the person who shows the trade-off.

The practices that make this stick are a short written change note for any mid-sprint addition, a visible backlog ordered by value rather than by who shouted loudest, and a habit of revisiting the original goal when a request arrives, because a request that does not serve the goal is easy to defer once the goal is in the room.
followUps: What do you do when a stakeholder insists the addition is urgent and free?
How do you justify a refactoring to a non-technical stakeholder?
tips: Turn every addition into a visible trade-off instead of a yes or no.
Translate technical work into the business outcome it protects.
commonMistakes: Absorbing extra work silently and then missing the deadline.
Arguing technical merit instead of business value when asking for engineering time.

interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: mentoring juniors and explaining tech to non-technical stakeholders
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: you are the senior on a team with junior developers, and you must also explain a risky technical decision to non-technical stakeholders. How do you handle both?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Mentor through small, reviewed, real work with clear goals; explain technical decisions to stakeholders in terms of risk, cost, and options, not implementation details.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Mentoring works through real work, not lectures. Give a junior a small, well-bounded task with a clear definition of done, review the work promptly with reasons rather than verdicts, and pair on the hard part so they see how a senior thinks through it, including the dead ends. Set a visible growth goal, such as owning a small feature end to end, and protect time for it instead of letting urgent work crowd it out every sprint. The signal that mentoring is working is independence: the junior starts asking better questions and needs fewer reviews for the same kind of task.

Explaining a risky decision to non-technical stakeholders uses the same discipline in reverse: start with the outcome and the risk, not the technology. Say what happens if you do it and if you do not, what it costs in time and money, and what the alternatives are, in plain language without jargon. A useful shape is options with trade-offs: the safe option, the fast option, and the recommended option, with the recommendation justified by the business risk it reduces. Invite questions rather than presenting a finished decision, because a stakeholder who understands the trade-off will defend it later.

Both jobs share one habit: check understanding instead of assuming it. Ask the junior to explain the design back to you, and ask stakeholders what worries them about the plan, because the worry they name is the one your explanation must answer.
followUps: How do you know when a junior is ready to own a feature alone?
What do you do when stakeholders reject your recommended option?
tips: Mentor with real tasks and prompt, reasoned reviews.
Present decisions as options with trade-offs, in business language.
commonMistakes: Mentoring only by reviewing finished code instead of pairing on the thinking.
Explaining the implementation instead of the risk, cost, and options.

practiceItems.explanation: Generics are a compile-time mechanism. After erasure both are just List at runtime, which is why you cannot do new T() or instanceof List<String>. This is also why a raw List can hold the wrong type and fail later with a ClassCastException.
options: They are two different classes at runtime.
They share the same runtime class, List; the type argument is not available at runtime.
The compiler rejects both in the same program.
Generic type arguments are checked again at runtime on every access.
practiceItems.prompt: What does Java's type erasure mean for List<String> and List<Integer> at runtime?
practiceItems.title: Type erasure

practiceItems.explanation: A lambda may capture only effectively final local variables, so it sees a stable snapshot rather than a changing variable. Because count++ modifies count, it is not effectively final and compilation fails. An array element or an AtomicInteger would be the usual workaround.
options: Lambdas cannot print variables.
Variables captured by a lambda must be effectively final, and count is modified after the lambda is created.
Runnable cannot be a lambda target.
count must be declared as var.
practiceItems.prompt: Why does this code fail to compile? int count = 0; Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(count); count++;
practiceItems.title: Lambda variable capture

practiceItems.explanation: get() on an empty Optional throws NoSuchElementException, so it defeats the purpose. orElseThrow, orElse, map and ifPresent force the empty case to be handled. Optional is designed as a return type, not as a field or method parameter, and returning null instead of empty defeats its contract.
options: Call get() directly; it never throws.
Use orElseThrow() or orElse / ifPresent to handle the empty case explicitly.
Store Optional as a field in every entity class.
Return null instead of Optional.empty().
practiceItems.prompt: Which is the recommended way to handle a possibly-absent value in Optional<String>?
practiceItems.title: Optional best practice

practiceItems.explanation: The default scope is singleton: the container creates one instance and shares it for every injection. prototype creates a new instance each time, while request and session scopes only apply in a web context. A singleton bean holding mutable per-request state is a common concurrency bug.
options: prototype: a new instance per injection.
singleton: one shared instance per Spring container.
request: one instance per HTTP request.
session: one instance per user session.
practiceItems.prompt: What is the default scope of a Spring bean, and what does it mean?
practiceItems.title: Default Spring bean scope

practiceItems.explanation: 201 Created is the precise code for a successful creation, and the Location header tells the client where the new resource lives. 200 is a generic success, 204 means success with no body (typical for DELETE), and 301 is a redirect, not a creation result.
options: 200 OK
204 No Content
201 Created, ideally with a Location header
301 Moved Permanently
practiceItems.prompt: A POST endpoint successfully creates a new resource. Which status code should it return?
practiceItems.title: Status code for creation

practiceItems.explanation: var only removes the redundant type name for local variables; the inferred type is fixed at compile time, so the variable cannot later hold another type. It requires an initializer, and it is not allowed for parameters, fields, or return types.
options: var makes Java dynamically typed.
var is local-variable type inference: the type is fixed at compile time from the initializer.
var can be used for method parameters and return types.
var variables can be declared without an initializer.
practiceItems.prompt: Which statement about Java's var is correct?
practiceItems.title: Local variable type inference

practiceItems.explanation: String is immutable, so + in a loop creates a new string on every iteration. StringBuilder mutates one buffer, and unlike StringBuffer it is not synchronized, so it is faster when only one thread uses it. StringBuffer is only needed when the buffer is genuinely shared across threads.
options: String concatenation with + in a loop, because it is fastest.
StringBuffer, because it is faster than StringBuilder.
StringBuilder, because it avoids creating many intermediate strings and has no synchronization overhead.
String, because it is mutable.
practiceItems.prompt: When building a string in a loop in single-threaded code, which should you prefer and why?
practiceItems.title: StringBuilder vs StringBuffer

practiceItems.back: Heap: objects and their fields, shared across threads, reclaimed by the garbage collector. Stack: one per thread, holds method frames, local variables and references; freed automatically when a method returns.
practiceItems.front: What lives on the heap vs the stack in Java?
practiceItems.title: Heap vs stack

practiceItems.back: Any resource declared in the try header that implements AutoCloseable is closed automatically at the end of the block, even if an exception is thrown, in reverse order of declaration.
practiceItems.front: What does try-with-resources guarantee?
practiceItems.title: Try-with-resources

practiceItems.back: Producer Extends, Consumer Super: use List<? extends T> when you only read T values out of the list, and List<? super T> when you only write T values into it.
practiceItems.front: What does PECS mean for wildcards?
practiceItems.title: PECS rule

practiceItems.back: Auto-configurations are conditional: @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty and similar conditions are evaluated, so a configuration only applies when its conditions hold and you have not provided your own bean.
practiceItems.front: How does Spring Boot decide whether to apply an auto-configuration?
practiceItems.title: How auto-configuration backs off

practiceItems.back: Set spring.profiles.active (for example, spring.profiles.active=prod) and annotate the bean or configuration with @Profile("prod"). Profile-specific properties live in application-prod.properties or application-prod.yml.
practiceItems.front: How do you activate a Spring profile and a profile-specific bean?
practiceItems.title: Spring profiles

practiceItems.back: A record is a compact, immutable data carrier class: the compiler generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString from its components, and records cannot extend another class.
practiceItems.front: What is a Java record, in one sentence?
practiceItems.title: Java records

practiceItems.description: Given a list of words, return a map from each word to the number of times it appears. Treat words case-sensitively and do not modify the input list.
hints: Map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) handles both first and repeat occurrences.
A stream with Collectors.groupingBy and counting() also works.
practiceItems.title: Word frequency count

practiceItems.description: Return a list of strings for numbers 1 to n inclusive: "FizzBuzz" for multiples of both 3 and 5, "Fizz" for multiples of 3 only, "Buzz" for multiples of 5 only, otherwise the number itself as a string. For n <= 0 return an empty list.
hints: Check the multiple-of-15 case before the multiple-of-3 and multiple-of-5 cases.
Use % to test divisibility.
practiceItems.title: FizzBuzz list

practiceItems.description: Return true if the given string reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring case but not ignoring other characters. An empty string counts as a palindrome; a null input returns false.
hints: Compare characters from both ends moving inward; you can stop at the first mismatch.
Lowercase the string once before comparing.
practiceItems.title: Palindrome check

practiceItems.description: Given a list of strings, group them by their length into a map from length to the list of words of that length, preserving the order words appear in the input.
hints: Collectors.groupingBy(String::length) does this in one pipeline.
The default groupingBy collector preserves encounter order within each group.
practiceItems.title: Group words by length

practiceItems.description: Given a list of integers, return a new list with duplicates removed, preserving the order of first occurrence. Do not modify the input list.
hints: Stream.distinct() preserves encounter order for ordered streams.
A LinkedHashSet also preserves first-occurrence order.
practiceItems.title: Remove duplicates preserving order

practiceItems.description: Write a BankAccount class with a private balance, a constructor taking an initial balance (reject negatives with IllegalArgumentException), deposit and withdraw methods (withdraw rejects amounts above the balance), and a getBalance method. Keep the balance encapsulated: no public field.
hints: Validate in the constructor and in each method, not only in one place.
deposit and withdraw should reject negative amounts too.
practiceItems.title: Encapsulated bank account

practiceItems.explanation: 7 / 2 is integer division, which truncates toward zero to 3. 7 / 2.0 promotes the division to double, giving 3.5. The other options confuse truncation with rounding (4) or apply floating-point division to both.
practiceItems.prompt: What does this code print?
practiceItems.title: Integer division output

practiceItems.explanation: After append the buffer is "abcdef". delete(1, 3) removes characters at indexes 1 and 2 (the end index is exclusive), i.e. 'b' and 'c', leaving "adef".
options: abcdef
adef
abef
aef
practiceItems.prompt: What does this code print?
practiceItems.title: StringBuilder delete output

practiceItems.explanation: A return in finally overrides the return value from try: the try block's 1 is set aside and the finally block's 2 is what the method actually returns. This is also why returning from finally is discouraged — it silently discards the try result and any exception in flight.
options: It does not compile
practiceItems.prompt: What does this code print? Assume getValue() is called from main and its result is printed.
practiceItems.title: Return in try and finally

practiceItems.code:
Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (c == d));
practiceItems.explanation: Autoboxed Integers in the range -128 to 127 are cached, so a and b are the same object and == is true. 128 is outside the cache, so c and d are distinct objects and == is false, even though equals would be true. Never use == to compare wrapper objects.
options: true true
true false
false true
false false
practiceItems.prompt: What does this code print?
practiceItems.title: Integer cache output

practiceItems.code:
int i = 5;
System.out.println(i++ + " " + ++i + " " + i);
practiceItems.explanation: i++ yields the old value 5, then i becomes 6. ++i increments first to 7 and yields 7. The final i is still 7. So the output is "5 7 7".
practiceItems.prompt: What does this code print?
practiceItems.title: Pre- and post-increment output

practiceItems.code:
String s = null;
System.out.println(s + "x");
practiceItems.explanation: String concatenation converts null to the literal text "null" instead of throwing, so the result is "nullx". Calling a method on s, such as s.length(), would throw NullPointerException — but + does not call a method on s.
options: NullPointerException
x
nullx
It does not compile
practiceItems.prompt: What does this code print?
practiceItems.title: Null string concatenation

practiceItems.description: ServiceA depends on ServiceB and ServiceB depends on ServiceA. The application fails to start with a circular reference error. How do you fix it properly, rather than just working around the error?
practiceItems.solution: First question whether the cycle is real: often one direction can be removed by extracting the shared logic into a third service both depend on, or by having one side depend on an event or interface instead of the concrete class. If a cycle is genuinely needed, inject one side lazily with @Lazy, or restructure so the shared behaviour lives in a separate bean. Avoid re-enabling circular references via spring.main.allow-circular-references as a permanent fix, since it hides a design problem and can leave partially-initialized beans.
practiceItems.title: Fixing a circular bean dependency

practiceItems.description: A report generator builds a large CSV by concatenating strings with + inside a loop over 100,000 rows, and it is very slow with high memory churn. Diagnose the cause and propose a fix.
practiceItems.solution: Because String is immutable, each + creates a new string and copies all previous content, giving quadratic copying and heavy garbage collection. Replace the loop body with a single StringBuilder created before the loop, append each row, and call toString() once at the end. For joining with a delimiter, StringJoiner or String.join / Collectors.joining are idiomatic alternatives.
practiceItems.title: Slow string building in a loop

practiceItems.description: A REST endpoint accepts a registration request and manually checks each field with if statements scattered through the service layer. Invalid data sometimes reaches the database. How would you restructure validation?
practiceItems.solution: Validate at the API boundary with Bean Validation: annotate the request DTO with constraints such as @NotBlank, @Email and @Size, add @Valid on the controller parameter, and handle failures centrally in a @ControllerAdvice that returns 400 with per-field errors. Keep business-rule checks (for example, whether an email is already registered) in the service layer, and keep the DTO separate from the entity so validation rules do not leak into persistence.
practiceItems.title: Validating a REST request

practiceItems.description: A service depends on a repository and an external client. The team writes only slow end-to-end tests, so feedback is slow and failures are hard to localize. Propose a testing approach for this service.
practiceItems.solution: Test the service in isolation as a unit test with the repository and client mocked (for example with Mockito), covering success, not-found and error paths quickly. Add a separate slice test (such as @DataJpaTest) for the repository's real queries, and a small number of end-to-end tests for the critical happy path only. Log with a correlation id so a failure in any layer can be traced, and keep test data builders so tests stay readable as cases grow.
practiceItems.title: Choosing a test for a service

practiceItems.explanation: Count++ is read-modify-write, so two threads can read the same value and both write back the same incremented value, losing one update. volatile only guarantees visibility of the latest write, not atomicity of a compound action. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() is atomic, and a lock would also work.
options: volatile makes count++ atomic.
The JVM reorders the loop body.
Two threads can interleave the read, increment and write of count++, losing an update.
AtomicInteger is slower, so the JVM skips updates.
practiceItems.prompt: A shared int counter incremented by two threads with volatile ends up below the expected total. Why?
practiceItems.title: Lost update with volatile

practiceItems.explanation: A fixed pool of 2 threads with an unbounded queue will accept tasks forever, so a burst can queue millions of tasks and exhaust memory. A bounded queue plus an explicit rejection policy (abort, caller-runs, or discard) makes overload visible and bounded. More threads alone only moves the bottleneck; shutting down the pool after submit is not a sizing fix.
options: Use a cached thread pool instead.
Increase the pool to 200 threads.
Use a bounded work queue with an explicit rejection policy, so overload is bounded and visible.
Submit tasks with invokeAll instead of submit.
practiceItems.prompt: A fixed pool of 2 threads with an unbounded queue runs out of memory under a burst of tasks. What is the best fix?
practiceItems.title: Executor queue sizing

practiceItems.explanation: The young generation is collected frequently and cheaply because most objects die young (the weak generational hypothesis); surviving objects are promoted to the old generation, which is collected rarely and more expensively. Tenuring thresholds control how many young collections an object survives before promotion.
options: Objects are allocated in the old generation first.
Most objects die young, so the young generation is collected often and cheaply, and survivors are promoted.
The young generation is never collected.
Promotion happens on every method call.
practiceItems.prompt: Why does the JVM split the heap into a young and an old generation?
practiceItems.title: Generational garbage collection

practiceItems.explanation: A JWT is signed, so the server can verify it without storing session state, but its claims cannot be changed after signing — the token stays valid until it expires. That is why access tokens are kept short-lived and revocation is handled by expiry plus refresh-token rotation, a denylist, or a version claim, rather than by editing the token.
options: Delete the token from the database.
You cannot edit a signed token; you must wait for expiry or use short lifetimes plus a revocation mechanism such as refresh rotation or a denylist.
Change the signing key for just that user.
Send the token a logout request.
practiceItems.prompt: A user's JWT must be invalidated immediately after logout. Why is this not as simple as deleting a session?
practiceItems.title: JWT revocation

practiceItems.explanation: Accessing a lazily loaded association after the persistence context (EntityManager / transaction) has closed throws LazyInitializationException, because there is no session left to fetch the data. Fetching the needed data inside the transaction with JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph, or mapping to a DTO inside the transaction, fixes it. Open Session in View hides the problem by keeping the session open into the view layer, at the cost of unpredictable queries.
options: The entity has no default constructor.
The lazy association is accessed after the persistence context has closed.
The association is annotated fetch = EAGER.
The query used a DTO projection.
practiceItems.prompt: What causes LazyInitializationException?
practiceItems.title: LazyInitializationException

practiceItems.explanation: A circuit breaker stops calling a failing downstream service after a threshold, fails fast, and periodically lets a trial call through to check recovery. Retrying immediately and forever amplifies the overload; adding threads only delays saturation; caching only helps if stale data is acceptable for that endpoint.
options: Retry every failed call immediately and indefinitely.
Increase the caller thread pool until the downstream recovers.
Trip a circuit breaker: fail fast after a failure threshold and probe periodically for recovery.
Cache every response permanently.
practiceItems.prompt: Service A calls a failing Service B, and retries pile up until A also collapses. Which pattern prevents this cascade?
practiceItems.title: Circuit breaker

practiceItems.explanation: PECS: producers use extends, consumers use super. You read numbers out of List<? extends Number>, so extends is right. With super you could only safely read Object values out. <?> (unbounded wildcard) also allows reading, but only as Object, losing the Number type.
options: List<? super Number>
List<Number>
List<? extends Number>
List<Object>
practiceItems.prompt: A method only reads numbers from a list parameter and must accept List<Integer> as well as List<Double>. Which parameter type is correct?
practiceItems.title: Wildcard for a producer

practiceItems.explanation: Buffered streams batch many small reads/writes into fewer system calls, which is the main win. try-with-resources still matters, but it closes the stream; it does not batch I/O. Files.readAllLines loads the whole file into memory, which is fine for small files but not for large ones, and NIO's Files.lines streams lazily.
options: Buffered streams compress the file.
Buffered streams batch small reads and writes into fewer system calls.
Buffered streams make files thread-safe.
Buffered streams load the entire file into memory.
practiceItems.prompt: Why wrap a FileInputStream in a BufferedInputStream?
practiceItems.title: Buffered I/O

practiceItems.back: Happens-before: a write to a volatile variable (or releasing a lock, or starting a thread) happens-before every subsequent read of that variable (or acquiring the same lock, or the started thread's actions). It is the guarantee that makes one thread's writes visible to another.
practiceItems.front: What is the happens-before relationship, in one sentence?
practiceItems.title: Happens-before

practiceItems.back: A stop-the-world pause is a period when application threads are stopped so the collector can safely reclaim memory. Long pauses hurt latency; collectors such as G1 and ZGC aim to keep pauses short and predictable, at the cost of more total CPU or memory.
practiceItems.front: What is a stop-the-world GC pause, and why does it matter?
practiceItems.title: Stop-the-world pauses

practiceItems.back: Access token: short-lived (minutes), sent with each request, proves identity. Refresh token: long-lived, stored securely, used only to obtain a new access token. Never put sensitive data in a JWT payload, because it is only base64-encoded, not encrypted.
practiceItems.front: Access token vs refresh token — and what must never go in a JWT payload?
practiceItems.title: Access vs refresh tokens

practiceItems.back: NIO's Files.lines(path) returns a lazily populated Stream<String> that must be closed (use try-with-resources). It does not load the whole file into memory, unlike Files.readAllLines.
practiceItems.front: How do you stream a large file line by line with NIO, and what must you remember?
practiceItems.title: Files.lines

practiceItems.description: Write a thread-safe counter class with increment() and get() methods that is correct under concurrent use by many threads, without using synchronized or explicit locks.
examples: 100 threads each calling increment() 1,000 times → get() returns 100,000
hints: AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() is a single atomic operation.
A plain int with volatile would still lose updates on increment.
practiceItems.title: Thread-safe counter

practiceItems.description: Write a generic method swap that swaps two elements in any list (any element type) given their indexes. Do not use raw types, and do not create a new list.
hints: Declare the method as <T> void swap(List<T> list, int i, int j).
List.set returns the previous element, which makes the swap concise.
practiceItems.title: Generic list swap

practiceItems.description: Copy a file from a source path to a destination path using NIO, replacing the destination if it already exists. The method must close all resources and propagate IOException to the caller (do not swallow it).
examples: copy("a.txt", "b.txt") copies the full contents of a.txt to b.txt
If b.txt already exists, it is replaced
hints: Files.copy(Path, Path, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING) does this in one call.
Convert String paths with Path.of(...).
practiceItems.title: Copy a file with NIO

practiceItems.description: Given a list of words, count occurrences of each word using multiple threads safely, without using synchronized blocks. Return a Map<String, Long> of word to count.
hints: ConcurrentHashMap.merge(word, 1L, Long::sum) is atomic per key.
parallelStream() can drive the concurrent updates, or use an explicit thread pool.
practiceItems.title: Concurrent word count

practiceItems.explanation: Because of type erasure, both lists are instances of the same runtime class (the List implementation class, e.g. List12 for List.of). The String vs Integer type argument exists only at compile time, so the classes are equal.
options: false
true
It does not compile
ClassCastException
practiceItems.prompt: What does this code print?
practiceItems.title: Generic erasure output

practiceItems.explanation: synchronized makes each increment atomic and gives mutual exclusion, so no update is lost. After both threads are joined, all 2,000 increments have happened, so get() deterministically returns 2000. Without synchronization or joining, the result could be lower or not yet complete.
options: A value between 1000 and 2000, varying by run
It throws ConcurrentModificationException
practiceItems.prompt: What does this program print?
practiceItems.title: Synchronized counter output

practiceItems.explanation: orElse takes a value, not a supplier, so its argument is evaluated eagerly before orElse is even called — "called" is printed even though the Optional is present. orElseGet(() -> defaultValue()) would be lazy and would not print "called" here.
options: real
called, then real (on two lines)
default
It does not compile
practiceItems.prompt: What does this code print?
practiceItems.title: Optional orElse eagerness

practiceItems.explanation: supplyAsync produces 5, the first thenApply doubles it to 10, the second formats it as "value=10", and join() waits for the chain and returns that string. join() unwraps failures as unchecked exceptions, unlike get(), which throws checked ones.
options: value=5
value=10
It prints nothing because the future never completes
practiceItems.prompt: What does this code print?
practiceItems.title: CompletableFuture chain output

practiceItems.description: Two threads each transfer money between the same two accounts, but in opposite directions, and the program sometimes hangs forever. Diagnose the problem and propose a fix that preserves correctness.
practiceItems.solution: This is deadlock: each thread holds one account's lock and waits for the other's. Fix it by imposing a single global lock order — for example, always lock the account with the smaller id first — so no thread can hold one lock while waiting for a lock another thread holds in the opposite order. Alternatives include using one lock per transfer operation, or tryLock with a timeout and retry, but a consistent lock order is the cleanest fix. Also verify with thread dumps that the hang is a lock cycle, not an infinite loop.
practiceItems.title: Deadlock in account transfers

practiceItems.description: A latency-sensitive service suffers periodic 2-second pauses, and GC logs show long old-generation collections. How do you investigate and reduce the pauses without guessing at flags?
practiceItems.solution: First confirm GC is the cause: enable GC logging (for example -Xlog:gc*) and correlate pause timestamps with the latency spikes. Then check what is being promoted: look for large short-lived allocations, oversized caches, or objects surviving because of long-lived references. Reduce allocation (reuse buffers, avoid boxing in hot paths, cap caches) before tuning the collector. If pauses remain, try a low-pause collector such as G1 with a pause-time goal or ZGC, and measure throughput and pause percentiles before and after — a collector change that fixes p99 at the cost of unacceptable throughput is not a win.
practiceItems.title: Diagnosing long GC pauses

practiceItems.description: A single-page app stores a long-lived JWT in localStorage and calls APIs with it. After a token theft incident, the team must redesign token handling. What should change, and what should stay?
practiceItems.solution: Move to short-lived access tokens (minutes) plus rotating refresh tokens: each refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, so a stolen refresh token is detected on reuse and the whole token family can be revoked. Store the refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie rather than localStorage where JavaScript can read it, and keep the short-lived access token in memory. Never put passwords, roles that must be revocable, or other sensitive data in the JWT payload, since it is only base64-encoded. Add a server-side revocation list or token version for immediate logout of compromised accounts.
practiceItems.title: Redesigning JWT handling after theft

practiceItems.description: A controller returns a JPA entity directly. The JSON serializer touches a lazily loaded collection and the request fails with LazyInitializationException in production but not in tests. Explain the difference and propose a fix.
practiceItems.solution: In tests the transaction (or Open Session in View) is often still open when serialization happens, so lazy loading succeeds; in production the transaction has closed before the serializer runs. Fix it properly: fetch exactly what the response needs inside the transaction — a JOIN FETCH query, an @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection — and return a DTO, not the entity. That also prevents leaking internal fields and accidental extra queries. Do not fix it by marking the association EAGER or by enabling Open Session in View in production, both of which hide the problem and cause unpredictable queries.
practiceItems.title: LazyInitializationException in production only

practiceItems.description: Checkout calls inventory, payment and notification services in sequence. When payment is slow, checkout threads block, timeouts cascade, and one slow service takes down the whole checkout flow. Propose a resilient design using timeouts, bulkheads and observability.
practiceItems.solution: Give every downstream call an explicit timeout (shorter than the caller's own timeout) so a slow service fails fast instead of holding threads. Isolate each dependency with a bulkhead — a dedicated thread pool or concurrency limit — so payment slowness cannot exhaust the pool used for inventory. Add a circuit breaker so repeated failures fail fast and recover gradually, and retry only idempotent calls with backoff and a cap. Make payment calls idempotent with an idempotency key so a retried request cannot double-charge. Expose health, metrics and traces (via Actuator and distributed tracing) so the slow dependency is visible before it cascades, and design the checkout to degrade gracefully — for example, queue the notification instead of blocking checkout on it.
practiceItems.title: Resilient checkout across microservices

practiceItems.explanation: Action deserves roughly 60% of the answer: it shows your steps, choices, and reasoning. Long background leaves nothing to score, and a result without actions is just a claim.
options: The Situation, so the interviewer understands all the background.
The Action, because it is the evidence of what you personally did.
The Result, because outcomes matter more than process.
The Task, because your job title explains your seniority.
practiceItems.prompt: In a well-structured STAR answer, which part should take the most time?
practiceItems.title: STAR time proportions

practiceItems.back: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Situation and Task set context, Action is the evidence of your contribution, and Result states the outcome and lesson.
practiceItems.front: What do the four letters of STAR stand for?
practiceItems.prompt: What do the four letters of STAR stand for?

practiceItems.description: A candidate answers 'Tell me about a time you handled a tight deadline' like this: 'We had a really busy period at work and everyone was stressed. The project was complicated and there were lots of stakeholders. We worked really hard and in the end we managed to deliver it, which was great.' Evaluate this answer and rewrite it into a strong STAR answer (use a clearly fictional scenario).
practiceItems.solution: Weaknesses: no specific situation, no personal task or role ('we' throughout), no concrete actions ('worked really hard' is not a step), and no measurable result. A strong rewrite: Situation — a fictional reporting tool had to launch in two weeks when its data source changed format. Task — the candidate owned the data-import part. Action — mapped the format differences, proposed a translation layer instead of rewriting every report, built it behind a flag, and compared old and new outputs on sample data. Result — launched on the original date with matching outputs, and the translation layer made the next format change take hours instead of days. Lesson: check external source stability early in planning.
practiceItems.prompt: A candidate answers 'Tell me about a time you handled a tight deadline' like this: 'We had a really busy period at work and everyone was stressed.

practiceItems.explanation: Humble-brag failures read as evasion: interviewers hear them constantly and score them as a refusal to answer. A real failure, owned plainly with a concrete lesson, scores far better.
options: A real failure with a clear account of your part and a specific behavior change afterwards.
A failure where the outcome was partial but the lesson is concrete.
A 'failure' that is secretly a strength, such as working too hard or caring too much.
A failure in which you misjudged a situation and explain what you would do differently.
practiceItems.prompt: Which answer to 'Tell me about a time you failed' is most likely to be scored poorly?
practiceItems.title: The failure question trap

practiceItems.back: Questions repeat competencies under different wordings. One story, re-emphasized, can answer leadership, challenge, ownership, and learning questions — so a small tagged story bank covers dozens of phrasings.
practiceItems.front: Why prepare a bank of six to eight stories instead of one answer per interview question?
practiceItems.prompt: Why prepare a bank of six to eight stories instead of one answer per interview question?

practiceItems.description: A candidate answers a conflict question by spending most of the answer explaining why their teammate's approach was wrong and how the candidate eventually proved them wrong. Improve this answer: what should change in tone, structure, and ending?
practiceItems.solution: Change the tone: describe the disagreement as a difference in view or priority, not as the teammate being wrong, and avoid blame or gossip. Change the structure: show listening first (what the teammate's concern was and why it was reasonable), then the discussion, then how a decision was reached. Change the ending: close with the resolution and the working relationship afterwards, plus what the candidate changed about how they handle disagreements — not with a victory lap.
practiceItems.prompt: A candidate answers a conflict question by spending most of the answer explaining why their teammate's approach was wrong and how the candidate eventually proved them wrong.

practiceItems.explanation: Lead with the problem: it gives the listener a reason to care about everything that follows. Technologies belong in the middle as decisions with reasons, and schemas and feature lists belong in follow-ups, not the opening.
options: A list of the frameworks and databases the project used.

practiceItems.description: An interviewer asks: 'What happens when your notification service goes down?' A candidate replies: 'It never goes down; we built it well.' Rewrite this into a strong deep-dive answer using a fictional booking system where notifications are sent asynchronously from a queue.
practiceItems.solution: A strong answer: bookings still succeed because the notification worker reads from a queue and is separate from the booking path, so a worker outage delays messages rather than losing bookings. On recovery, queued notifications are retried and delivered. Detection comes from queue-depth and worker-health alerts. The deliberate trade-off: delaying an email was judged acceptable, losing a booking was not. If the queue itself failed, bookings would still be recorded but notifications would need a replay from booking records — that is the residual risk, and it is why queue durability was chosen over speed.

practiceItems.description: Evaluate and improve this trade-off answer: 'We used one database for everything because it was simpler. It worked fine.' Use a fictional internal tool as the setting and supply the missing parts.
practiceItems.solution: Missing parts: genuine alternatives, the deciding constraint, the cost, and the revisit condition. Improved version: Decision — one database for the application and its reporting layer. Alternative — a separate reporting store fed by a pipeline, which would isolate reporting load. Deciding constraint — a small team, a short deadline, and modest reporting volume (a few dozen reports a day). Cost — a heavy report could slow the main application, managed with report-size limits and scheduling heavy reports outside working hours. Revisit condition — at roughly ten times the reporting volume, the separate store becomes the right call, and that trigger was documented for the team.

practiceItems.description: Write a SQL query that returns each customer who has placed at least 3 non-cancelled orders, with their order count and total spend, ordered by total spend descending. Tables: customers (id, email), orders (id, customer_id, total_amount, status).

examples.input: orders: customer 1 has 4 orders totalling 500, customer 2 has 2 orders totalling 900
examples.output: Only customer 1 appears, with order_count 4 and total_spent 500

hints: Filter cancelled orders with WHERE before grouping.
Use GROUP BY customer_id with COUNT(*) and SUM(total_amount).
Filter groups with HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3, not WHERE.
practiceItems.solution:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count, SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent
FROM orders
WHERE status <> 'CANCELLED'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
practiceItems.prompt: Write a SQL query that returns each customer who has placed at least 3 non-cancelled orders, with their order count and total spend, ordered by total spend descending.

practiceItems.description: Write a SQL query that returns the id and email of every customer who has never placed an order. Tables: customers (id, email), orders (id, customer_id).

examples.input: customers 1 and 2; only customer 1 has an order

hints: Use a LEFT JOIN from customers to orders.
Filter for rows where the joined order side is NULL.
practiceItems.solution:
SELECT c.id, c.email
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

practiceItems.description: Users report that after updating their profile name, the old name keeps showing for up to an hour. The profile is cached in Redis with a 1-hour TTL, and the update path writes to the database but does not touch the cache. Diagnose the problem and propose a fix that keeps caching benefits.
practiceItems.solution: Diagnosis: the cache is stale because the update path never invalidates the cached entry, so reads keep serving the old value until the TTL expires. Fix: evict (or update) the cached profile key in the same code path that writes the database, for example with Spring's @CacheEvict on the update method keyed by user id. Keep the TTL as a safety net for any missed invalidation, and consider a shorter TTL for frequently changed profile data. Verify with a test that updates the profile and then reads it back through the cache.
practiceItems.prompt: Users report that after updating their profile name, the old name keeps showing for up to an hour.

practiceItems.description: You are modelling a blogging platform in MongoDB. Each post has comments, and popular posts can accumulate tens of thousands of comments over years. Should comments be embedded in the post document or stored as separate documents referenced by post id? Justify your choice and note the trade-off.
practiceItems.solution: Store comments as separate documents referenced by post id. Embedding suits bounded data read together with the parent, but a comment list that grows without bound will hit the 16 MB document limit, make every comment addition rewrite a huge document, and slow post reads that do not need comments. Referencing keeps post documents small and stable, lets comments be paginated and indexed independently, and costs an extra query (or aggregation) to load a page of comments, which is the correct trade-off here. A small embedded summary, such as a comment count, can be maintained on the post if needed.
practiceItems.prompt: You are modelling a blogging platform in MongoDB.

practiceItems.description: A team wants to move its order and payment data from PostgreSQL to a document store 'for scalability', although current load is modest and the main complaints are slow reports and occasional double-charges. Evaluate the proposal and recommend an approach.
practiceItems.solution: Do not migrate the transactional core: orders and payments need multi-row ACID transactions, integrity constraints, and join-heavy reporting, which PostgreSQL serves well and a document store serves poorly. The symptoms point elsewhere: slow reports suggest missing indexes or N+1-style query problems, and double-charges suggest missing idempotency or transaction boundaries, not the wrong database family. Fix those first, measure, and only consider a second store for a workload that genuinely fits it, such as a document store for the product catalogue or Redis for caching, keeping PostgreSQL as the system of record for orders and payments.

practiceItems.answer: So dependency downloads are cached in their own layer and reused when only source code changes.

Copying source first would invalidate the dependency layer on every code change and force a full re-download. There is no rule requiring pom.xml first, RUN can be followed by COPY, and multi-stage builds keep source out of the final image.

So dependency downloads are cached in their own layer and reused when only source code changes.
Because source code cannot be copied after a RUN instruction.
Because it makes the final image contain the source code.

Because pod IPs change when pods are replaced, so clients need a stable DNS name routing to current healthy pods.

Rebuilding is possible and images can cross environments; the issue is correctness, not feasibility.

practiceItems.description: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for a Spring Boot application built with Maven. The build stage must compile the jar, the runtime stage must contain only a JRE and the jar, dependencies must be cached before source is copied, and the container must run as a non-root user with an exec-form entrypoint exposing port 8080.
examples: Input: a Maven project with pom.xml and src/ → Output: an image that runs the Spring Boot jar on port 8080 without Maven or source code in the final image
hints: Copy pom.xml and download dependencies in their own layer before copying src/.
Use COPY --from=build to bring only the jar into the runtime stage.
Create a user and switch to it with USER before ENTRYPOINT.
practiceItems.solution:
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN ./mvnw -q dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/myapp-1.0.0.jar app.jar
RUN groupadd -r appgroup && useradd -r -g appgroup appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
practiceItems.title: Multi-stage Dockerfile for Spring Boot

practiceItems.description: Write a GitHub Actions workflow that runs on pushes to main and on pull requests, sets up JDK 21 with a Maven cache, runs the full build and tests, then builds and pushes a container image tagged with the commit SHA. Secrets must not appear in the file.
examples: Input: a push to main → Output: build and tests run, then an image tagged with the commit SHA is pushed to the registry
hints: Trigger on push to main and on pull_request.
Use actions/setup-java with java-version 21 and cache maven.
Tag the image with github.sha so every image traces to one commit.
practiceItems.solution:
name: build-and-test
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up JDK 21
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          java-version: "21"
          distribution: temurin
          cache: maven
      - name: Build and test
        run: ./mvnw -q verify
      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t <your-registry>/order-service:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Push image
        run: docker push <your-registry>/order-service:${{ github.sha }}
practiceItems.title: CI pipeline for a Java service

practiceItems.description: Write a Kubernetes Deployment for a Spring Boot service named order-service with 3 replicas, a pinned image version, container port 8080, a prod Spring profile via environment variable, memory and CPU requests and limits, and liveness and readiness probes using Actuator endpoints.
examples: Input: image <your-registry>/order-service:1.2.0 → Output: 3 healthy replicas behind matching labels, receiving traffic only when ready
hints: The Deployment selector must match the pod template labels.
Use /actuator/health/liveness for liveness and /actuator/health/readiness for readiness.
Set requests for scheduling and limits as a cap, with heap sized inside the memory limit.
practiceItems.solution:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-service
          image: <your-registry>/order-service:1.2.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
              value: "prod"
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "512Mi"
              cpu: "250m"
            limits:
              memory: "1Gi"
              cpu: "500m"
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health/liveness
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 10
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health/readiness
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 5
practiceItems.title: Kubernetes Deployment for Spring Boot

practiceItems.description: A teammate copied a credentials file into a Docker image in one layer and deleted it in a later layer, believing the secret was gone. The image was pushed to the registry. What is the real situation, and what must the team do now?
practiceItems.solution: The secret is still in the image: layers are immutable, and the earlier layer containing the file remains in the image history and can be retrieved. Deleting in a later layer only hides it from the final filesystem view. The team must rotate the exposed credential immediately, rebuild the image without the secret ever being copied in, push the clean image, and remove the tainted image from the registry. Going forward, secrets arrive at run time via environment variables or a secret store, never via COPY or ENV in a Dockerfile.
practiceItems.title: Secret found in an image layer

practiceItems.description: Your team's CI pipeline fails intermittently on the same few tests, and developers have started rerunning the pipeline until it goes green. What is wrong with this habit, and what should the team do instead?
practiceItems.solution: Retrying until green destroys trust in CI: real failures get retried away alongside flaky ones, and the suite stops being evidence that a change is safe. The team should quarantine the flaky tests, reproduce the flakiness, and fix the root cause — usually timing assumptions, shared mutable state, test-order dependence, or reliance on an external service. Only deterministic tests return to the suite, and a pattern of retries on one test is treated as a bug to fix, not a normal workflow.
practiceItems.title: Flaky tests in CI

practiceItems.description: After a rolling update on AWS, error rates spike for a Spring Boot service, but the new containers pass their basic liveness checks. How should the team respond, and what made a fast rollback possible?
practiceItems.solution: Roll back first and investigate second: redeploy the previous known-good image, which the rolling update kept available, rather than hot-fixing production under pressure. Liveness only proves the process is alive, not that it serves correctly, which is why error-rate and latency alarms, readiness checks, and smoke tests matter. The rollback was possible because images are tagged by version and kept in the registry, the previous task definition or Deployment revision was retained, and configuration is separate from the image, so the old image runs correctly with current configuration.
practiceItems.title: Rolling back a bad AWS deployment
